              Operational highlights - investment




Operational highlights – investments
Investment strategy and core principles
Our investment strategy is designed to deliver sustainable, long-term, risk-adjusted returns for policyholders and
shareholders, within the Group’s risk appetite. It is anchored in disciplined ALM and a robust risk governance
framework aligned with our strategic objectives and regulatory requirements. We aim to meet our financial
obligations to shareholders, the reasonable expectations of policyholders, and regulatory capital requirements.
The strategy reflects product characteristics and capital needs across each Business Unit and the Group. Every
investment decision begins with the nature of the long-dated liabilities, rather than potential asset returns in
isolation. Core principles of our investment strategy are:

(i)     Capital preservation: Policyholders, debt holders and shareholders entrust us with their capital; therefore,
        safeguarding it is paramount within our investment strategy.

(ii)    Unlocking illiquidity premium: Given the long-term nature of our liabilities, we look to capture illiquidity
        premia in private markets to deliver better returns for our stakeholders.

(iii) Risk-first approach: Risk-based capital charges are broadly proportional to potential volatility. Where we
      lack clear visibility on appropriate risk-adjusted returns, we hedge or avoid the exposure.

Strategic partnership model for Asset Management
The asset management industry has evolved rapidly over the past decade, with specialist asset managers
emerging, such as in private assets, ESG, quantitative strategies, and others expanding alongside consolidation
among traditional firms.

Against this backdrop, we employ a core-satellite strategic partnership model that combines in-house
capabilities with leading external asset managers to deliver value for our stakeholders. This collaborative
approach is integrated into our Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA) and Tactical Asset Allocation (TAA) processes
and informs product pricing. It is designed to enhance policyholder returns, improve shareholder outcomes and
maintain balance sheet discipline.

• Core in-house capabilities: Asset-liability management expertise, manager selection, efficient allocation and
       operations, and strong governance to manage conflicts of interest.

• Asset manager partnerships: Engagement of internationally reputable external managers to access secular
       growth opportunities, deploy yield-enhancement strategies and gain exposure to traditional assets while
       minimising fund costs.

This model enables agile asset allocation across Business Units to ensure appropriate alignment with our
liabilities.

Strategic Asset Allocation
Our portfolio management follows a two-tiered structure: SAA sets long-term asset mix targets based on liability
profiles, capital needs, and the market outlook; and TAA allows short-term adjustments to capture market
opportunities while operating within Board defined risk limits. Execution combines internal expertise with
external managers for specialised asset classes to deliver outcomes expected by stakeholders.

Asset-Liability Management
Asset-liability management is overseen by dedicated committees at both Group and Business Unit levels under
our enterprise risk management (ERM) framework and ALM policy, and operating within Board defined risk
limits. Key actions include matching asset duration to liability profiles, hedging interest-rate and currency
exposures where economically optimal, and managing discretionary policyholder benefits and product pricing to
mitigate volatility. Together, these measures support returns, financial resilience and long-term value creation.

ESG integration
We embed ESG considerations into our investment process to manage high ESG risks and build resilient and
sustainable investment performance over the long term.

Operational highlights – digital & technology
Technological innovation is at the core of FWD Group’s business strategy. The Company takes a customer-led
approach across the entire insurance journey, harnessing integrated, scalable, and a modular technology
architecture complemented by AI, advanced data analytics, and cloud computing.

Scalable, cost-efficient operational platforms
FWD’s operational efficiency is based on a cloud-native, modular architecture that drives scalability and cost
optimisation. FWD Opus, our operations management platform, integrates with FWD Omne and FWD Cube to
deliver end-to-end automation for new business underwriting, policy servicing, and claims. This approach aims
to increase volumes to be handled with the same or fewer resources while improving turnaround times for
underwriting, policy servicing, and claims.

Our OneMod architecture standardises technology modules across markets, enabling application programming
interface (API)-driven integration and legacy system retirement. OneMod has digitised end-to-end insurance
processing which has enabled us to decommission all our legacy applications. As part of our cloud-first project,
99 per cent of utilised applications were migrated to cloud as at 31 December 2025.

The OneMod platform has successfully unified the customer and operations platforms, and experience across
Japan, Thailand, Cambodia, the Philippines and Indonesia, as well as enabled instant capabilities across
servicing, claims and new business sales. For example, through OneMod, FWD Thailand has been able to
provide advanced capabilities like instant claims payment for over 15 per cent of total claims through the FWD
Omne app. Furthermore, FWD Japan has improved operational efficiency through the reduction of over 20 per
cent of the unit cost for claims assessment and management.
These platforms operate on FWD’s cloud environment, which helps ensure security, resilience, and strong data
governance. This transformation has accelerated software development and deployment, reduced time-to-
market, and improved reliability. Automated infrastructure provisioning has shortened operational lead times
and enhanced consistency across markets, delivering a robust foundation for scalable, cost-efficient growth.

Advanced data analytics and generative AI execution
FWD Group’s digital and technology strategy is anchored in a data-driven approach, with AI and analytics
embedded across operations to enhance decision-making, automation, and customer experience. By the end of
2025, FWD operated over 320 active AI models, the number of which has increased by 50 per cent from two
years ago, reflecting the rapid scale-up of AI-powered tools across the enterprise. The core of this
transformation is FWD’s proprietary One Data Platform, which processed close to 600,000 data points and
curates more than 10,000 attributes for the customer view in real time across all our markets. This platform
underpins all active AI models and more than 100 in-house applications, enabling end-to-end visibility and data-
driven decisions across the business.

Our AI capabilities extend beyond operational efficiency to risk management and profitability. For example,
FWD’s AI fraud detection system, fully integrated into claims platforms in Hong Kong, Thailand, and Japan,
monitors claims in real time to identify anomalies and prevent fraud, safeguarding both the company and
customers. These enhancements accelerate the legitimation of claim settlements, often instantly via the FWD
Omne app, while reducing leakage from the fraudulent claims. Furthermore, AI-powered lapse prevention
models prioritise at-risk policies for proactive engagement and, in 2025, prevented the lapse of policies resulting
in US$30 million of APE savings from policies at risk of surrender.

As we scale advanced data and generative AI capabilities, FWD remains committed to responsible AI practices.
Our Responsible AI Standards, guided by seven principles of fairness, accuracy, accountability, transparency,
auditability, explainability, and human-centricity, aim to ensure ethical deployment and mitigate bias.
Governance is reinforced through market-level AI and Data Committees and a Group AI and Data Sub-
committee, established to ensure consistency, compliance, and risk oversight. Complementing this, our
Technology & Operations Academy fosters lifelong learning, with employees completing about 20,000 courses
and earning over 1,100 certifications since 2021.

Customer experience and digital platforms
FWD Group is committed to making insurance simple, fast, and intuitive by embedding digital innovation across
every customer and partner touchpoint. We have built a suite of advanced platforms and tools that transform

FWD Vision AI automates data extraction and document authentication with 92 per cent optical character
recognition accuracy, enabling fast onboarding and remote selling. For example, in Japan, generative AI in
underwriting reduced case review time by 40 per cent and 98 per cent of complex cases were automated by the
end of 2025. Claims are streamlined through the FWD Omne app, which processes low-risk claims instantly
using AI-powered fraud detection and optical character recognition. This innovation helped to achieve a claims
NPS of 80 and over 92 per cent of “Great” and “Good” customer servicing emotion in 2025.

Singapore, reducing manual call handling efforts and shortening customer wait time. These 24/7 assistants

cent in 2024 to 20 per cent in 2025, and call centre seats were cut by 45 per cent from 2021, reflecting cost
savings from voicebot and digital initiatives.

Digital distribution and sales enablement
Our tech-enabled distribution strategy blends the human touch of agents and partners with powerful digital
tools. At its core is FWD Cube, our proprietary agency management platform accessible via tablet, web, or
mobile. It consolidates financial needs analysis, quotations, e-submissions, and automated underwriting into one
intuitive interface.
Generative AI powers our AI Agent Assistant and virtual coach that help agents understand customer needs,
identify opportunities, and improve conversion. In the Philippines, our agents using our AI Agent Assistant,
achieved over 10 per cent higher APE production compared to non-users in 2025, demonstrating measurable
productivity gains through adopting AI for distribution force.

In 2025, we introduced the Advisor and Customer Engagement (ACE) tool within FWD Cube, leveraging
generative AI for lead generation and personalised content creation. ACE enables agents to engage prospects
quickly, while agency leaders benefit from real-time dashboards for team performance insights.

Our strength in digital extends to bancassurance. In Thailand, FWD was able to integrate our own customer tool
FWD Omne with SCB’s banking app SCB Easy within a six-month timeframe, integrating our insurance products
access into the bank’s mobile ecosystem. Similar integration models are being deployed across other bank and
ecosystem partners, enabling shared data-driven campaigns and streamlined purchase journeys. These
initiatives exemplify how FWD’s digital distribution strategy broadens reach, enhances productivity, and delivers
enhanced experiences for customers and partners alike.

Operational highlights – customers
Turning customer-centric vision into reality
Customers are at the heart of everything we do, and our ambition is to be the most customer-led insurer in every
market we serve. This commitment is embedded across our operations, from product design to service delivery.
In 2025, we further strengthened our customer-first strategy, earning external recognition, with FWD’s NPS
ranking among top three in five out of eight markets1.

Customer experience across key markets remains strong, with purchase emotion score remaining high at 92 per
cent2, reflecting our focus on seamless and supportive interactions. Claims NPS reached a robust 63 points in
2025, underscoring our continued progress in delivering fast, transparent, and empathetic claims experiences.

We also remain focused on proactively reducing customer complaints through regular training and raising
awareness across teams. Our complaint ratio – measured as the number of complaints received per transaction
over a calendar year – has remained consistently low at around 0.2 per cent for each year between 2022 and
2025. Together, these outcomes reinforce our unwavering commitment to put customers first and to
continuously enhance service excellence.

Redefining customer ease through digital innovation
FWD accelerated its digital transformation journey in 2025, delivering tangible improvements in customer
experience and operational efficiency across markets. We achieved a 73 per cent e-submission rate across
customer purchase, service and claims journeys, with 91 per cent of new business applications submitted
digitally, up from 86 per cent in 2024. Our continued focus on paperless, mobile-first and electronic
Know-Your-Customer solutions has enhanced customer convenience while enabling scalable efficiency across
the organisation.

End-to-end STP increased to 47 per cent, from 40 per cent in 2024, supported by sustained progress across
purchase, service and claims journeys. In parallel, our Fraud, Waste and Abuse detection model was deployed in
Hong Kong, Thailand and Japan, further strengthening trust and reliability in our claims processes.

Innovation and technology remain central to FWD’s customer-centric strategy. Our FWD Omne app continues to
empower customers through instant claims and real-time engagement, earning the Customer Experience
Excellence Award at the InsurInnovator Connect Asia 2025 Awards. In Hong Kong, FWD MAX further deepens
customer relationships by creating more meaningful and connected experiences.

In 2025, we expanded digital engagement through local messaging platforms to meet customers where they are.
In Indonesia, FWD became the first life insurer to enable customers to purchase digital insurance products via
WhatsApp. We have also introduced WhatsApp as a channel to re-engage customers with abandoned
applications in Hong Kong.

Together, these achievements underscore FWD’s strength in customer experience, digital innovation and
operational excellence, as we continue redefining ease and confidence for our customers across every
interaction.

Driving customer value and loyalty
FWD’s efforts to deepen customer relationships continued to deliver strong results. In 2025, 31 per cent of new
policies were sold to existing policyholders – up from 24 per cent in 2024 – demonstrating the effectiveness of
our cross-sell and up-sell strategies and the growing strength of customer loyalty.

Looking ahead, we remain focused on delivering relevant and personalised solutions that anticipate evolving
customer needs and maximise lifetime value across every stage of the customer journey. Over 2025, we made
solid progress towards this ambition by accelerating our digitalisation agenda, deepening customer
engagement, and setting new benchmarks for innovation and service excellence.

We remain committed to empowering customers as we advance our vision of changing the way people feel
about insurance.

to learn the foundational processes and managers’ responsibilities that are mapped to the employee life cycle.

The content is bespoke but anchored on essential leadership capabilities, including understanding self, building
trust and psychological safety within teams, leading through change, cultivating a growth mindset, living values
and purpose, and navigating cross-cultural ways of working.

To maximise engagement and impact, the programmes adopt a hybrid learning model that blends classroom
training, peer learning, and experiential methods such as simulations and gamification – designed for immersive
and practical learning experiences.

We complement these programmes with Forum 55, our biannual leadership forum for executive leaders. Forum
55 brings together over 100 of our senior executives in person to engage in key strategic topics shaping FWD’s
future. The forum features a mix of internal and external speakers, fostering dialogue, collaboration, and fresh
perspectives that strengthen leadership alignment and strategic execution across the Group.


Foster a learning culture for re-skilling and up-skilling
FWD continues to invest in holistic development for all employees through education sponsorships, mandatory
compliance training, and enterprise-wide access to Anytime Learning which includes LinkedIn Learning’s
20,000+ courses. Since launching Anytime Learning in 2022, employees have completed over 138,863 courses,
with a 95 per cent activation rate and strong engagement in trending topics such as generative AI. In 2025, we
prioritised integrating AI-driven tools into our platform, including AI role-play features designed to help users
enhance everyday work conversations. Since launching this capability, learners have engaged in over 3,000
simulated conversations, driving meaningful skill development across the organisation.

In 2025, we strengthened our learning culture with:

• Annual Learning Festival: a virtual event engaging more than 1,000 employees on trending soft skills and AI
   capabilities.

• Anytime Learning Newsletter: leaders model continuous learning by sharing how they leverage Anytime
   Learning resources.

Individual development goals remain embedded in quarterly manager-employee conversations, reinforcing our
commitment to future-ready talent.

AI-First Mindset and Customer-Centricity
The GenAI Hub continues to serve as a go-to resource for employees, providing curated learning materials on
generative AI and related topics. In 2025, FWD strengthened its commitment to an AI-first mindset by leveraging
the Microsoft suite of AI tools as our primary platform. To accelerate adoption, we hosted regular webinars on
practical Microsoft AI tips and featured AI-focused sessions during our Annual Learning Festival, equipping
employees with the skills to enhance productivity and innovation.

At the same time, we have continued to develop human skills that complement the AI-first approach – such as
curiosity, problem-solving, adaptability, and resilience – ensuring our workforce remains agile and future-ready.

As a customer-led insurer with a dedicated focus on putting the customer at the heart of everything we do, a
series of Customer Experience webinars were hosted to empower employees with strategies and tools to deliver
exceptional service and create best-in-class experiences for our customers.

Attract, motivate and retain talent
Remuneration policy
Our remuneration philosophy is consistent with our business strategy and capital management strategies. It aims
to align the achievement of our business results with individual remuneration outcomes, while also recognising
individual contributions. Our remuneration policy ensures that the total remuneration packages we offer enable
us to attract, motivate and retain the highly talented individuals our business needs, who will drive the future
success of FWD Group. We also seek to promote sound and effective risk management measures in relation to
remuneration practices that align with our culture and values as an organisation. We use a combination of short-
term and long-term incentives to ensure our employees and senior management are aligned with our strategy
and deliver the right results. Please see details of these incentives in the section headed “Corporate governance
— Remuneration report” in this annual report.

Employee retention
Across the Group, our voluntary employee turnover1 was 10.8 per cent in 2025, down from 12.3 per cent in 2024.
This was achieved through the implementation of various employee retention strategies including: talent
development, learning platforms and programmes, the FWD LiveLife well-being strategy and initiatives, our DEI
strategy, and Community Care, among others. The relatively consistent employee turnover rate has enabled us
to develop a more stable, experienced, productive, and engaged workforce, while also reducing recruitment and
training costs.

Environmental, social and governance
Our ESG strategy
As a pan-Asian insurer, we seek to embed ESG values into our culture and decision-making to align business
success with creating meaningful impact for our shareholders, customers, employees, and communities. Our
ESG strategy is designed to guide materially important decisions across our operations, from product design to
investments and processes, and focuses on delivering a vision underpinned by three strategic pillars: (1)
accessible protection solutions for underserved customers, (2) investing responsibly for sustainable growth, and
(3) upholding governance practices that build trust and transparency.

1. Accessible protection
We are committed to closing the protection gap by offering affordable, inclusive life and health insurance across
our markets in Asia. In 2025, we launched our Inclusive Insurance Framework to expand access through simpler
products, digital platforms, and partnerships with community organisations.

Beyond product innovation, we actively promote financial literacy and well-being. In 2025, we supported over
64,700 individuals through programmes that strengthened financial knowledge and resilience.

2. Sustainable investment
We embed sustainable investment practices across our portfolios to create long-term value for our stakeholders.
Our philosophy balances the focus on returns with ESG integration, manages risk, and aims to reduce exposure
to high environmental impact sectors.

In 2025, we introduced our Climate Action Plan to mitigate climate risks through engagement and to allocate
capital to climate and sustainable investments.

3. Effective governance and sustainable business
We uphold good corporate governance and promote sustainable practices across our operations. Sustainability
within our business includes managing our operational emissions and addressing climate risks across our
investment portfolio. Our governance framework ensures effective oversight as a regulated insurance group,
prioritising long-term shareholder value and the interests of customers, regulators, and partners.

Guided by our PICCO values, we want to attract and retain talent to drive industry progress. Through
responsible practices and robust governance, we aim to create positive impact for the millions of lives we serve.

Creating impact
Our approach aligns with six United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) where we can create lasting
impact: SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic
Growth), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and SDG 13 (Climate
Action).

Materiality assessment approach
Our vision of changing the way people feel about insurance relies on strong stakeholder relationships. We
engage openly and transparently to understand diverse needs, identify emerging risks, and keep our ESG
strategy focused and relevant. To achieve this, we adopt a multi-channel approach, interacting regularly with
internal and external stakeholders through the channels outlined below:

organisations                     • Meetings and conferences
                                  • Membership and networking events


Feedback from stakeholders informs our materiality assessment, helping to identify and validate ESG issues that
are most critical to our business and society. We refresh this process regularly through structured engagement
with senior management and the Board.

In 2024, we refreshed our materiality assessment using research on ESG trends, industry practices, and
reporting frameworks, followed by over 20 stakeholder discussions and workshops to gain deeper insight. This
feedback guided our ESG strategy and prioritised areas where we could create the greatest impact.

In 2025, we reviewed the selected ESG issues for relevance. The refreshed assessment was endorsed by our
Group Executive Committee (GEC) and approved by the Nomination Committee, informing our annual ESG
reporting.

Empowering customers and communities through
accessible protection
Asia faces one of the world’s most pressing protection gaps, with many households vulnerable to financial
shocks. A recent study estimated that combined health and mortality gaps had reached US$390 billion in 20241,
a 26 per cent increase since 2017. The health gap alone stood at US$258 billion, driven by rising medical costs,
ageing populations, and high out-of-pocket spending, while the mortality gap surged to US$132 billion in
premium equivalent terms in 2024, a 35 per cent increase from 2017. Despite progress in distribution and
underwriting, insurance penetration has remained low in emerging markets2, leaving families exposed.

Our 2025 consumer outlook survey revealed that cost-of-living inflation, rising medical expenses, and income
uncertainty remained as key financial concerns for our customers, highlighting the need for affordable,
accessible insurance solutions that provide a safety net for families. Since our inception, we have been
reimagining the insurance journey by addressing real pain points and challenging traditional models. In 2025, our
brand continues to be recognised for being “different” (YouGov BrandIndex) and our customer-led innovation
was acknowledged through external awards for simpler, faster and more intuitive customer journeys.

We continue to improve customer outcomes through our Operations Excellence Community by simplifying
processes and embedding best practices across all customer touchpoints. Digital access remains to be an
enabler of accessible, efficient and consistent customer experiences across markets. Our integrated digital
platforms, FWD Omne, FWD Cube, FWD Opus, and OneMod, support seamless engagement across purchasing,
servicing, claims handling and value-added service. Building on these efforts, we launched our Inclusive
Insurance Framework in 2025 to guide the design of simple and inclusive products, leverage digital platforms,
and partner with communities to build trust and awareness.

Led by our Accessible Protection Working Group, the Inclusive Insurance Framework brings together experts
across functions to reimagine protection through life stages and scale commercially viable solutions.

Inclusive and accessible products and services
We focus on three aspects of accessibility:

Affordability – offering options for different income segments

Awareness – helping customers understand their needs and how insurance can help

Availability – ensuring suitable products are widely accessible to meet their needs

To achieve this, the following examples demonstrate how we are designing inclusive offerings for underserved
communities, including low-income groups, persons with disabilities and chronic conditions, and those at high
health risks, with highlights of our products and services in 2025.

Engaging with the community
FWD Group takes a long-term view in empowering communities with the knowledge, confidence, and skills to
live fulfilling lives while building trust in Asia’s growing life insurance industry. We recognise financial literacy is a
key enabler for accessible protection and we take a holistic approach to well-being in our community initiatives
– spanning financial health, physical and mental wellness, and social entrepreneurship.

Through our Community Care programme, in 2025, we supported over 64,700 individuals through large-scale
financial education and inclusion programmes, alongside local grants focused on health and well-being. In 2025,
employees across the Group brought one of our core values, of caring, to life. Our people contributed 11,200
volunteering hours, up 35 per cent from 2024, across a range of meaningful community and charitable initiatives.

We also responded holistically to support the Tai Po community in Hong Kong, following the devastating fire in
late 2025. In addition to the direct support provided to our affected customers, FWD also pledged HK$10 million
to support the wider community. A portion of these funds were donated in December 2025 to the Hong Kong
Council of Social Services and Habitat for Humanity Hong Kong to support immediate community needs. The
remaining funds will be allocated in 2026 for longer-term recovery efforts. FWD Group also introduced its first
employee donation matching programme, supporting six local charities – Crossroads Foundation, Feeding Hong
Kong, Habitat for Humanity Hong Kong, Mind HK, The Mission for Migrant Workers, and Yan Chai Hospital –

Financial education and literacy
Financial literacy is critical to economic development, yet awareness and education remain low. We believe that
introducing financial education early in life helps to build healthy money habits and empowers young people to
make informed choices.

                         In 2025, FWD extended its three-year partnership with Junior Achievement (JA)
                         Worldwide to continue the award-winning pan-Asian JA SparktheDream programme.
                         The initiative aims to equip students across Asia with the skills and tools they need to
                         take charge of their financial future.

From 2022 to 2024, the programme reached over 37,000 students, with 88 per cent gaining an understanding of
the role of money in daily life and 80 per cent developing greater community awareness. In the next phase, from
2025 to 2027, the aim is to educate another 40,000 students across seven markets in Asia, integrating financial
education with social and life skills, deepening engagement with parents and teachers, and introducing
initiatives to build mental health resilience.

In 2025, the programme reached more than 13,700 students with the support of more than 400 FWD volunteers.
Over 170 student teams participated in the annual JA SparktheDream Social Challenge where they put their new
skills and creativity into practice to solve real-world challenges in their communities. Our senior leaders across
FWD Group also dedicated an afternoon during a management conference in Hong Kong, for the largest single
session completed to date in the JA SparktheDream programme, with 150 local primary school students.

Building climate resilience in our business
Asia is estimated to drive 60 per cent of global growth in 20251. The ASEAN2 region, home to seven of our
markets, has over 680 million people, a combined gross domestic product (GDP) of US$3.9 trillion3. By 2030, it is
expected to become the world’s fourth-largest economy4.

This rapid progress has brought prosperity and innovation, but has also heightened climate vulnerabilities driven
by urbanisation and resource demands. Climate change is causing more frequent and intense extreme weather
events, while rising temperatures threaten health and food security through reduced agricultural productivity
and the spread of diseases. The cost of inaction is high, prompting policy makers and businesses to accelerate
adaptation strategies.

We see climate and customer resilience as deeply interconnected. Closing protection gaps and creating impact
requires innovation, agility, and partnership. To support this, we embed environmental sustainability into
operations - reducing greenhouse gas emissions, conserving resources, and strengthening stewardship across
the business.

Within our investment portfolio, sustainable investing is central to this approach. Beyond integrating ESG risks
and opportunities, we focus on decarbonising the portfolio to drive long-term value creation and support the
transition to a low-carbon economy.

Together, these efforts strengthen our ability to provide reliable protection in a region increasingly exposed to
climate risks and impacts. We are also enhancing climate-related disclosures referencing the Task Force on
Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations, covering our climate strategy, risk
management, targets, and performance metrics.


Climate governance
The Board holds ultimate accountability for the Group’s ESG approach, which includes oversight of climate
strategy and management of climate-related risks and opportunities. Board-level committees, the GEC, and
specialised functions support this oversight. The Risk Committee advises on identifying, measuring, and
managing material climate risks, while the Nomination Committee ensures climate considerations are integrated
into director nominations to maintain relevant expertise.

Climate risk is embedded in FWD’s ERM process, guided by our Climate Risk Management Policy, which defines
principles and roles across the Group. The GEC provides quarterly ESG updates, including climate-related
initiatives, to the Board through the Nomination Committee, while the Risk Committee reports when there are
significant risk changes. Progress against climate objectives is regularly monitored to ensure alignment with ESG
priorities and strategy. In 2025, external experts delivered training to the Board, focused on climate trends, risks
and opportunities. A portion of performance-related compensation is determined for employees in the Group
ESG function who are responsible for driving ESG within the organisation, with reference to the goals outlined
by our ESG strategy.

Further details on FWD’s ESG governance can be found on page 83; further information on FWD’s Risk
Management governance and Three Lines of Defence approach to risk management can be found in the section
headed “Financial and Operating Review — Risk Management”; and further information on FWD’s remuneration
framework can be found in the section headed “Corporate governance — Remuneration report” in this annual
report.

Climate risk management
The management of climate risk is part of the overall Group ERM framework. Further details on FWD's ERM
framework can be found in the section headed “Financial and Operating Review — Risk Management” in this
annual report.

Climate-related risks and opportunities
As a pan-Asian insurer, climate risks increasingly shape our strategy, business, and operations. To anticipate
potential impacts, we conducted a climate risk assessment covering physical, transition, and liability risks.
Climate risks often emerge over longer timeframes than traditional reporting captures. We categorise these as:

• Short-term: 0 to 1 year
• Medium-term: 1 to 5 years
• Long-term: 5+ years
Our assessment indicates higher risks in countries with significant coastal exposure and dense populations, as
well as in our investment portfolio, which includes carbon-intensive sectors. While climate change presents
multiple challenges, we have prioritised the most relevant risks for life and health insurers.

Scenario analysis and stress testing
We conducted a company-wide climate scenario analysis across our business planning period, referencing
global standards, including Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios, and benchmarked
against industry practices. To align with evolving standards, we expanded from two to three scenarios:

• Delayed Transition: Countries and sectors experience delays in implementing necessary policy changes.
   Climate policies are divergent across countries and sectors, leading to fragmented efforts. Carbon prices are
   typically higher in this scenario due to policy delays and lack of coordination.

• Current Policies (Hothouse World): Existing climate policies remain largely unchanged with low global effort
   to halt global warming. This leads to irreversible climate damage as temperature thresholds are exceeded.

• Fragmented World: Geopolitical tensions and a fragmented transition failing to contain physical risks,
   leading to supply chain disruptions, increased market volatility, and uneven progress towards emission-
   reduction targets.

These scenarios were selected to help assess vulnerabilities across our business model, investment portfolio, and
long-term resilience.

The Delayed Transition scenario highlighted risks from abrupt policy shifts and market volatility, critical for
assessing transition risk exposure in our investments and underwriting.

The Hothouse World scenario reflected severe physical risks such as more frequent extreme weather events
which could affect claims experience, operational continuity, and customer needs.

The Fragmented World scenario illustrated the compounded impact of geopolitical fragmentation and delayed
climate action, amplifying both transition and physical risks across our operations and value chain.

By analysing these scenarios, we assessed vulnerabilities across our value chain and tested the resilience of our
strategy under regulatory and physical stress conditions, ensuring readiness over the short, medium, and long
term.

The assessment highlighted key impact areas, particularly risks from new climate regulations, the Company’s
ability to transition, and potential effects on our investment portfolio. For example, exposure to energy and
utilities sectors could face increasing regulatory, investor, and reputational pressure, making transition risks
central to our sustainable investment and climate risk approach.

In line with our commitments, we track operational greenhouse gas emissions and explore sustainable asset
opportunities, with progress monitored regularly. Climate risk scenarios are integrated into Group Prescribed
Scenarios for ORSA, business planning stress tests, and scenario analysis. This strengthens our understanding of
climate impacts and informs strategies to mitigate risks, supporting a transition to a low-carbon, sustainable
society.


Climate targets and milestones: transitioning towards a low-carbon
economy
FWD’s climate action strategy aims to support global efforts to transition towards a lower-carbon economy by
2050 in an orderly, just, and inclusive manner.

We track environmental performance through our value creation scorecard, monitor operational emissions
across Scope 1 (direct emissions from natural gas and combustion from our own vehicles) and Scope 2 (indirect
emissions from purchase of electricity). Emissions are calculated using the GHG Protocol and reported under
both location- and market-based methods.

For 2025, electricity consumption has remained the largest contributor to Scope 1 and 2 emissions, at about 90
per cent, with the remainder from mobile fuel use.

Sustainable investment
As a long-term insurance and savings provider, our customers and stakeholders trust us to deliver life protection
and stable, long-term financial returns to allow them to celebrate living and secure a better future for themselves
and their families. To maintain this trust and build resilient and sustainable investment performance over the
long-term, we integrate ESG factors into our investment decisions.

Since becoming a signatory to the United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) in 2020, we have
committed to responsible investment as essential for long-term value creation and supporting a sustainable,
inclusive global economy. Our progress is detailed in our publicly available PRI Transparency report.


Managing ESG risks in our investments
We have strengthened our investment approach through policies addressing material issues such as human
rights, governance, climate change, and natural capital. Our Sustainable Investment Guidelines (SIG) act as the
first line of defence, screening investments for ESG risks which include United Nations Global Compact (UNGC)
and human rights violations, tobacco producers, ESG underperformers, high carbon emitters, controversial
weapons, and commodities like thermal coal and palm oil. We screen using a leading external data provider and
apply exclusions or thresholds. The SIG is publicly available on our website.

In 2025, over 90 per cent of our investments were screened for ESG risks1.


Engagement over exclusion
As an asset owner in the Asian markets, engagement is our preferred approach to mitigate long-term transition
risk and protect investment returns.

In 2024, we enhanced reporting with managers, focusing on quarterly screening and engagement for high ESG-
risk issuers. Once identified, we engaged through external managers or jointly, encouraging dialogue at board or
senior management level to address underperformance. Our methodology sets clear requirements for reporting,
outcomes, follow-up actions, and timelines. We also collaborate with investor organisations to share knowledge
and amplify impact.

We laid the foundation for climate action in 2021, with our first SIG, followed by strategy implementation in
2022-2023, including carbon footprint measurement using the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials
(PCAF) methodology, ESG provisions in mandates, and public reporting through our first UN PRI submission.


Strategic focus on high emitters
We recognise the need for an inclusive transition to a low-carbon economy, particularly in the Asian markets
where we operate. To accelerate investment portfolio decarbonisation, we prioritised engagement with the
highest-emitting companies, which account for 65 per cent of portfolio emissions1, following our stewardship
framework which categorises issuers by net zero2 alignment and transition risk.

In 2021, to reduce emissions and manage transition risks, we committed to phasing out thermal coal mining and
extraction from our investments and exiting by 20303. Since then, no new investments have been made and we
continue to run-off existing holdings.

As at 31 December 2025, our exposure to investments held in thermal coal mining and extraction companies has
reduced to US$54 million in 2025 from US$64 million the prior year. We have also assessed that the outstanding
corporate bonds we own will mature before the 2030 target.

Our climate action plan
To manage Scope 3 financed emissions with a view to decarbonise our portfolio, we have introduced a Climate
Action Plan covering three areas:

• Engagement with the top 20 issuers with the highest owned emissions or covering 65 per cent of our
   portfolio's emissions, and assessing outcomes;

• Reinvestment criteria favouring greener assets or low transition risk issuers, provided drivers of return and
   relative value are favourable; and

• Capital allocation to green assets, climate-aligned opportunities, transition enablers, and nature based
   solutions which could meet our environmental, social and return objectives.

Our aim is to balance emissions reduction with supporting transition efforts in the markets in which we operate.
We encourage our managers to prioritise issuers aligned with our sustainability goals and manage exposures to
those with higher transition risk.

Effective governance and sustainable business
Across our markets, we are guided by our Code of Ethics and Business Conduct, and our philosophy of Doing
the Right Things Right.

Our ERM framework enables us to identify, assess, and manage financial and non-financial risks, including ESG
and climate-related risks. It covers risk governance, management processes, and is reviewed annually to remain
fit for purpose. Controls and processes safeguard our business and customer assets, with the framework applied
across all Group Offices and Business Units.

Good governance is supported by exceptional people. Managing talent is central to our strategy, hence we
invest in employee development to foster an inclusive and ethical culture, and equip teams with skills to navigate
a rapidly changing environment. By empowering our people, we strengthen our ability to deliver on our vision
and create long-term stakeholder value.

Further details on our ERM framework can be found in the section headed “Financial and Operating Review —

ESG governance
The Board holds ultimate accountability for the Group’s ESG approach and strategy. Supporting the Board is the
GEC, comprising senior management led by the Group CEO, which sets and approves ESG ambition and
strategy, monitors performance, addresses emerging risks and opportunities, and makes recommendations to
the Board. The GEC reports quarterly to the Board on ESG updates, including those on trends, risks and
opportunities, sustainable investments and regulatory requirements through the Nomination Committee.

Additionally, the Risk Committee advises the Board on the identification, measurement, monitoring, and
management of material ESG risks as part of the ERM process, while the Group Risk function establishes ESG
risk methodologies and assessment processes under the ERM framework and provides updates on significant
developments.

Ensuring financial integrity
FWD is committed to preventing money laundering, terrorist financing, bribery, and corruption. The Group is
subject to anti-money laundering laws and regulations, as well as business conduct rules, in each or the
jurisdictions in which it operates. Further, the Group’s geographic diversification may increase its exposure to
the risk of violations of anti-corruption or similar laws.

Our internal controls include Group Anti-Money Laundering/Counter Terrorist Financing and Sanctions Policy,
Anti-Bribery and Corruption Policy, supporting standards, guidelines, and mandatory training. Compliance
teams conduct periodic Enterprise-wide Risk Assessments (EWRA) to identify and manage risks, with reviews at
least every two years or as required by local regulations. Programmes are subject to regulatory inspections and
internal audits.

We leverage technology to strengthen our anti-money laundering (AML) and counter terrorist financing (CTF)
framework, including name screening for sanctions, adverse news, and politically exposed persons, supported
by fuzzy logic and transliteration functions. Additional tools for transaction monitoring and customer risk rating
complement internal controls.

Oversight rests with each Business Unit’s Board, supported by timely compliance reporting. At Group level, the
Group Compliance and Operational Risk Committee (CORC) oversees policies and monitors risks through
regular reviews and management reports.

Employees play a key role in compliance. New hires complete onboarding financial crime training, while all staff
and the Board attend mandatory annual refresher sessions and focused workshops where applicable.

Whistleblowing
We foster a culture of honesty and integrity, encouraging employees to speak up when something feels wrong.
Our whistleblowing programme provides confidential reporting channels in every market, including an online
Speak Up platform and dedicated hotlines managed by an independent third party. Whistleblowers remain
anonymous to ensure confidentiality and prevent retaliation.

All reports are handled under the Group Investigation Procedure Manual to ensure fair, independent
investigations and appropriate follow-up. Final case resolutions are recorded confidentially in Speak Up Online.
The Group Chief Compliance Officer reports investigation progress and outcomes to the Audit Committee
quarterly.

Safeguarding trust through fair customer outcomes
Treating customers fairly
Conduct risks are inherent in insurance and could arise at any stage of the customer journey, from product
development to marketing, claims and complaints.

Our strategy places customers at the centre, supported by strong governance and compliance to ensure fair
treatment throughout the customer journey. The FWD Group Treating Customers Fairly Policy, integrated across
all Business Units and overseen by our Board, sets clear behavioural standards for employees and distribution
partners to deliver positive outcomes. All employees, contractors, and sales personnel also complete mandatory
training on the policy.

Responsible product development
Our responsible product development approach ensures fair and transparent design and distribution aligned
with customer needs and regulatory standards. This commitment spans the entire lifecycle, from concept and
pricing to communication and claims, embedding governance and customer-centric principles.

Pre-launch, we perform thorough due diligence, assessing commercial viability, target segment alignment,
distribution channels, financial metrics, and risk appetite. This process involves local and Group governance
through committees and functions such as Proposition, Actuarial, Underwriting, Investment, Risk, and
Compliance, ensuring every proposition is evaluated holistically. To further align with ESG objectives, we
integrate sustainability considerations into product approval and review processes, aiming to meet financial
targets and contribute positively to society.

Post-launch we review, gathering feedback to confirm intended outcomes, and implement improvements.
Customers should be able to easily understand the insurance they buy. We have simplified policies by removing
jargon through initiatives such as Project Clarity, which rewrote contracts in plain language, applied user
experience principles, and used visual aids to highlight key information. These changes have improved customer
understanding, enhanced product appeal, and enabled faster, more accurate support.

We have also removed exclusions based on outdated medical data and unsupported judgments, improving
underwriting and risk assessment. By simplifying policy language and reducing exclusions, we believe customers
can better understand their coverage and feel confident about making claims.

Responsible selling practices
We are committed to selling products in a fair, clear, and transparent manner, ensuring customers understand
what they purchase throughout the product lifecycle. Alongside the Treating Customers Fairly training, our
Group Distribution team and Sales Quality Policy set standards for recruitment, sales quality controls, and
compliance across all distribution channels.

The policy requires comprehensive training for our sales force on compliance, product features, and mandatory
requirements. It applies to all Business Units, including agents, financial advisors, and telemarketers, while
partners such as banks, brokers, digital distribution platforms and third-party call centres are also expected to
follow its principles and comply with regulatory obligations.

To protect customer interests, each Business Unit defines criteria for vulnerable customers and implements
safeguards. The CORC monitors practices, key risk indicators, and distribution misconduct, reporting quarterly
to the Risk Committee to maintain strong governance and accountability.

We also invest in professional and leadership development of our agency and distribution partners through
programmes with INSEAD Business School, LIMRA & LOMA trade associations, and initiatives supporting agents
to qualify for the MDRT, raising standards and strengthening customer relationships.

Further details on how we use digital innovation to enable timely, compliant sales and customer engagement can
be found in the section headed “Management discussion and analysis — Operational highlights - digital &
technology” and further information on our agency training programmes can be found in the section headed
“Management discussion and analysis — Operational highlights — distribution” in this annual report.

Dealing with customer complaints
We aim to meet customers’ expectations while delivering high-quality service. Our Group Customer Complaints
Policy governs the end-to-end process for handling complaints, ensuring fairness, timeliness, and compliance
with local regulations, under oversight of the CORC.

We provide accessible channels – hotlines, email, live chat, and social media – for customers to raise concerns.
Feedback is promptly acknowledged and addressed in line with guidelines to ensure fair outcomes. We
investigate complaints and analyse root causes and trends to continuously improve our products and services.

Further details on our complaint ratio can be found in the section headed “Management discussion and analysis
— Operational highlights — customer” in this annual report.

Strengthening cyber resilience
Data privacy and protection
Protecting personal data entrusted to us by customers, employees, partners, and third parties is a top priority.
We align our policies with leading data protection standards, require third-party compliance, and notify
customers of any Privacy Policy changes promptly.

Oversight is provided by the Board, supported by CORC and Group Compliance. Each FWD entity appoints a
Data Protection Officer and implements a Privacy Compliance Programme to meet local laws such as Hong
Kong’s Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance and Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Act. We also assess agency
and distribution partners for compliance.

Our Group Data Privacy Policy and Standards, outline principles for collecting, using, storing, transferring, and
disposing of personal data and sensitive personal data. These apply to all employees, contractors, and third
parties processing data on FWD’s behalf. Mandatory training ensures staff and contractors understand key
privacy concepts and how to protect information and systems.

Our efforts in respect of ensuring we uphold the highest standards of personal data protection and privacy has
been recognised and further details on our awards can be found in the section headed “Overview — About FWD
— Awards and recognition” in this annual report.

Information security (Cyber)
FWD recognises the evolving cyber threat landscape and is committed to safeguarding information assets.
Oversight is provided by the Board and senior management, supported by the CORC and our Group Chief
Information Security Officer (CISO) and Business Unit Information Security Officers.

The Group Office, led by the Group CISO, provides strategic direction and Group-wide governance for
information security. It establishes the Group Information Security Policy and Standards and drives the
standardisation of security controls, technologies and processes across markets. Cybersecurity risk is embedded
within the Group ERM framework, aligned to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and ISO/
IEC 27001 standard. Periodic assessments are conducted to evaluate maturity and identify areas for continuous
improvements.

To strengthen awareness, all employees complete mandatory annual cybersecurity training, and cyber
simulations, supported by targeted campaigns and Cybersecurity Awareness Month. We invest in defensive
technologies, processes, and skilled resources, complemented by partnerships with leading security providers.
Disaster Recovery Plans ensure business continuity and restoration of critical systems.

In 2025, FWD achieved ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification for our Group Office and three markets, demonstrating
our commitment to global best practices and our continued progress towards group-wide certification.

Responsible AI
As we scale advanced data and generative AI capabilities, FWD remains committed to responsible AI practices.
Our Responsible AI Standards are guided by seven principles of fairness, accuracy, accountability, transparency,
auditability, explainability, and human-centricity, to mitigate bias and ensure ethical deployment. Governance is
reinforced through market-level AI and Data Committees, and a Group AI and Data Sub-Committee, helping to
ensure compliance, consistency, and robust risk oversight.

About the ESG section
This is FWD’s fourth disclosure on our ESG strategy and performance. As an insurance provider, we recognise
our responsibility to support the well-being of our customers, employees, and communities while managing our
environmental and social impacts and upholding good governance practices. Unless otherwise specified, this
report covers the activities and initiatives from 1 January to 31 December 2025 across all Business Units under
our operational control in 10 Asian markets – Hong Kong, Macau, Thailand, Cambodia, Japan, the Philippines,
Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam and Malaysia – as well as a representative office in Mainland China. The
reporting scope excludes distribution channels that are not under the direct operational control of the Company,
including individual agents and bancassurance partners.

Our ESG disclosures reflect our commitment to transparency and accountability, providing our stakeholders
with a clear view of how we create long-term value responsibly. We manage material ESG issues and report
performance with reference to the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Universal Standards, the Sustainability
Accounting Standards Board (SASB) Standard for the Insurance sector and the recommendations of the TCFD. In
addition, our reporting meets the requirements set out in Appendix C2 Environmental, Social and Governance
Reporting Code under the Rules Governing the Listing of Securities on The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong
Limited (HKEX ESG Reporting Code).

  Balance                      We report information in a transparent and unbiased manner that provides fair
                               representation of both our positive and negative impacts.

Risk management
FWD Group has established a comprehensive risk management framework, including a risk management
committee structure and robust risk management frameworks, policies and strategies. Our risk management
framework is designed to ensure that the risks we have undertaken are backed by appropriate levels of capital to
support our ongoing business and protect all our stakeholders. We aim to balance efficient capital structures in
each of our operating insurance subsidiaries within acceptable levels of risk without compromising either
financial strength or our requirement for appropriate returns.

We have developed an ERM framework, which also incorporates our strategic objectives. This defines our risk
appetite, and the reliable practices to support a mindful risk culture at each level of the Group, namely every
director, officer, employee, agent or contractor.

Risk culture – and tone from the top
Our risk culture is the foundation of sound decision-making and sustainable growth. It reflects the shared values,
attitudes, and behaviours that guide how we identify, assess, and manage risk across the organisation.

We aim to maintain a risk culture that enables proactive risk management. We measure and strengthen this
culture through four key indicators: Tone, Accountability, Incentive and Competence.

Tone from the top remains critical in shaping risk awareness. Senior leadership communicates risk priorities and
demonstrates ethical decision-making, ensuring alignment throughout the organisation. Accountability is
promoted in our governance structure, with roles and responsibilities that promote ownership of risk decisions
and timely escalation of issues. Incentives are designed to encourage prudent risk-taking, linking performance
outcomes to behaviours that align with our risk appetite, while discouraging excessive risk-taking. Finally,
competence is reinforced through continuous training and development, equipping employees with the
knowledge and skills to make informed decisions and respond effectively to emerging risks.

During 2025, we advanced our Risk Culture Programme through targeted interventions and measurable
outcomes. A Risk Culture Survey was rolled out across all Business Units, supported by focus group discussions
to validate findings. Initiatives included enhanced risk and compliance training, leadership engagement sessions,
and integration of risk accountabilities into performance management frameworks. To reinforce desired
behaviours, we have in place our Risk and Compliance Key Performance Indicator.

Our Risk and Compliance Key Performance Indicator tool
We also have tools in place including a survey to measure the effectiveness of our risk culture. Our Risk and
Compliance Key Performance Indicator is set up to encourage all staff to demonstrate proper behaviours, to
manage risk within the approved tolerance, and escalate issues accordingly.

The Risk and Compliance Key Performance Indicator evaluates performance across four dimensions: adherence
to the Risk Appetite Framework (RAF), proactive risk and internal control management, compliance with
governance standards, and ethical conduct. These efforts aim to ensure continuous improvement and embed
risk awareness into everyday decision-making.

The annual calculation and final results of the Risk and Compliance Key Performance Indicator are approved by
the Risk Committee and Compensation Committee.


Risk governance
As part of the Group’s overall approach to maintaining robust corporate governance, our risk governance is
organised around the following principles:

• clearly established roles and responsibilities, and accountability;
• independent and properly resourced risk management and compliance functions; and
• our Three Lines of Defence.
Please refer to the section headed “Corporate governance — Corporate governance report” in this annual report
for further details in relation to our overall corporate governance arrangements.


Board of Directors
The Board takes ultimate responsibility for the risk management activities of FWD Group. It is responsible for
reviewing and approving strategies, plans and our risk appetite. It therefore plays a critical role in ensuring sound
and prudent policies and practices are in effect for ensuring good governance – and has continuous oversight of
risk management, internal controls and compliance matters.

To support the Board in carrying out these responsibilities, the following Board committees have been
established:

• Risk Committee
• Audit Committee
• Compensation Committee
• Nomination and Corporate Governance Committee
Further details on the work of the committees can be found in the section headed “Corporate governance —
Corporate governance report” in this annual report.


Management committees
To support the Risk Committee in carrying out its responsibilities, the following management committees have
been established to oversee the management of all risks:

Asset Liability Management Committee
The Asset Liability Management Committee (ALMCO) supports the Risk Committee with financial, investment,
liquidity and insurance risk oversight and ALM. The primary duties and responsibilities of the ALMCO are to: (i)
review and recommend major business unit’s SAA and TAA for Risk Committee approval; (ii) monitor the
effectiveness and implementation of the Group’s policies and related procedures for ALM; (iii) review and
approve formulation and execution of investment strategy; (iv) review and approve new classes of investment;
and significant hedging programmes; (v) monitor and review investment performance; (vi) monitor and review
the liquidity and investment exposures of Business Units and Group; (vii) immediately report and escalate



                                                                                                                        91
 Overview    Financial and operating review   Corporate governance    Financial statements   Additional information

                     Risk management




financial and insurance risk issues to the Risk Committee as appropriate; and (viii) provide advice on financial
and insurance risk management to the Risk Committee and the Board.

Compliance and Operational Risk Committee
The CORC supports the Risk Committee with its primary duties and responsibilities being to: (i) provide
direction, policies and oversight on management of non-financial risks, including but not limited to information
technology, cybersecurity and outsourcing risk, in line with the risk appetite set by the Board; (ii) immediately
report and escalate non-financial risk related issues to the Risk Committee as appropriate; and (iii) provide
advice on non-financial risk management to the Risk Committee and the Board.


Three Lines of Defence
The Three Lines of Defence structure aims to oversee, challenge and offer assurance across all business matters
in relation to risk. It ensures our control functions operate independently – and are properly resourced. The roles
and responsibilities of each are as follows:

First Line of Defence
The First Line represents the business operations, the management and employees who manage risk day-to-day
in accordance with the strategies and risk appetite set by the Board. The First Line develops and implements risk
mitigation actions – including monitoring and reporting any risks incurred in the course of business.

Senior management team

This is our executive management team and this team is responsible for effective internal controls and risk
management. The team regularly monitors and evaluates our overall risk profile to ensure that we operate within
our risk tolerance. The team takes an active role in managing risk by assessment, challenging where appropriate,
providing resolution plans as necessary, and capturing the results.

Functional units

Key personnel and management across functional units serve as process owners and risk takers responsible for
operating the business, and managing risks. This includes identifying, assessing, measuring, monitoring and
reporting risks associated with their business processes or functions, as well as executing business controls so
the overall business processes achieve their common objectives. The functional units translate the business risk
appetite into methodologies and policies to monitor business management’s control of risk.

Financial control function

The responsibilities for ensuring robust control over financial matters (e.g. investments, accounting and financial
reporting) are assumed by the Group Chief Financial Officer and undertaken by multiple teams under his control.
The responsibilities are assigned to ensure that: (i) suitable policies are developed, implemented and reviewed to
govern financial reporting and accounting practices; (ii) robust processes are designed, implemented and
reviewed to comprehensively manage financial transactions, financial reporting, protect financial resources and
reduce exposure to potential fraud; and (iii) adequate financial reporting systems and tools are established, with
integrated controls to identify any errors, inconsistencies or other accounting issues.

Actuarial function

The Actuarial function is established to provide advice to the Board and Group senior management regarding
matters on technical provisions, premium and pricing activities, actuarial modelling, capital adequacy,
reinsurance and compliance with related statutory and regulatory requirements, at a minimum.

 Overview    Financial and operating review   Corporate governance   Financial statements   Additional information

                   Risk management




Second Line of Defence
The Second Line comprises our risk management and compliance functions. These provide independent
oversight of risk exposures, risk management practices and compliance matters.

Risk Management

The Risk Management function is responsible for facilitating functional units in managing their risks and
coordinating risk management across the Group. Risk Management works collaboratively with other Second
Line functions to provide objective challenge and support and escalate matters when necessary – to help
optimise the trade-off between risk and reward.

The Risk Management function has responsibility for providing support and opinion to the Board, the Risk
Committee and the senior management team. This is to establish and implement appropriate policies and
procedures in relation to the Group ERM framework. The Risk Management function and the Group Chief Risk
Officer are responsible for the preparation of the ORSA report and actively liaise with the broader business and
executives to enable its timely delivery. The Group Chief Risk Officer has direct access to the Risk Committee
and Board for all risk matters independently and has a reporting line to the Chair of the Risk Committee.

Compliance

The Compliance function advises and assists functional units to manage compliance risk, ensuring compliance
with all applicable laws, regulations and ethical standards. Compliance (i) partners with the legal function to
identify laws, regulations and standards and identify areas of compliance risk within the business; (ii) works
closely with all functional units to identify activities to mitigate compliance risk based on the Board’s approved
risk appetite; (iii) monitors the First Line’s control of compliance risk and advises management on significant
compliance matters; (iv) works collaboratively with risk management to provide objective challenge and to
support and escalate matters when necessary to help optimise the trade-off between risk and reward; and (v) is
an adviser to the business as it designs, implements and embeds business procedures, tracks internal mitigation
activities, designs and delivers training and executes other framework activities. The Group Chief Compliance
Officer has direct access to the Risk Committee and Board for all compliance matters independently and has a
reporting line to the Chair of the Risk Committee.

Third Line of Defence
The Third Line comprises the internal audit function. It provides independent assurance on the design and
effectiveness of our risk management and internal control system. Internal Audit is independent of both the First
and Second Line functions and reports directly to the Audit Committee.

Risk Appetite Framework
The RAF organises the Group’s overall approach to selecting the risks it wishes to seek, retain, transfer and/or
avoid in the pursuit of its strategic objectives and guides key business activities accordingly. The RAF is
comprised of the risk philosophy, Risk Appetite Statements (RAS) and risk metrics and limits. Each of these
components are further supported by robust governance – i.e. roles, responsibilities and escalation mechanisms.

Risk philosophy: FWD Group’s risk philosophy defines the Group’s overall attitude towards risk, with
consideration of our vision, corporate strategy and the expectations of key stakeholders. The risk philosophy
therefore demonstrates a critical linkage between FWD’s business strategy and its approach to risk
management.

Risk Appetite Statements: FWD Group’s RAS and corresponding Actionable Statements set out the level of risk
that the Board is willing to accept in the pursuit of its strategic objectives and the actions to be taken in order to
remain within the risk appetite, respectively. The RAS are defined for each material risk to which the Company is
exposed in the pursuit of its key objectives.

Risk metrics and limits: FWD Group’s risk metrics and limits provide the capability for FWD to measure its
actual exposures relative to the Group’s RAS, evaluate the extent to which day-to-day business activities are
within the bounds of the risk appetite and determine whether any mitigation actions are required.

Risk management process
FWD has defined the risk management process in five steps:
                                                                                                   Risk identification


(i)    risk identification;

(ii)   risk assessment;
                                                                        Communication
(iii) risk response;
                                                                                                                                       Risk assessment
                                                                        & improvement




(iv) risk monitoring and review; and

(v)    communication and improvement.

The risk management process enables the Group to
identify the risks it is exposed to and provides guidance
on how the risks are to be mitigated or transferred.                             Risk monitoring
                                                                                    & review                                Risk response




Risk identification: We undertake risk identification to systematically and comprehensively identify any risks in
our processes, leveraging our people, tools and capabilities to capture the risks that the FWD Group is exposed
to.

Risk assessment: Risk assessment is performed by classifying risks into different levels. We then assess the
impacts against their inherent, residual and expected risks – considering the current control environment and
future mitigation actions.

Risk response: Based on the results of risk assessment, response measures are determined to manage risk in
accordance with our risk appetite.

Risk monitoring and review: Risk monitoring describes our process of assessing whether the FWD Group is in
control of its risks. Risk monitoring is a continuous process to measure and evaluate the effectiveness of our
internal controls; to determine whether any risks are within our risk appetite and in line with our desired levels;
and whether policies, minimum standards and regulations continue to be adhered to.

Communication and improvement: Risk information is gathered, analysed and communicated in a structured
way within our governance structures to ensure the relevant personnel are made aware of risks and can support
them in taking responsibility for managing risks.


Own Risk and Solvency Assessment
The Board and senior management team are responsible for the ORSA. This includes adopting a rigorous process
for setting, approving, and overseeing implementation of the ORSA. The Board and senior management team are
accountable for the ORSA report by reviewing and challenging its results – including the identification and
assessment of risks and the underlying assumptions for capital calculations.

                     Risk management




Principal risks
The FWD Group’s non-exhaustive principal risks are detailed below:

Strategic risks
Strategic risks cover corporate level issues the FWD Group faces, particularly those related to the
competitiveness and sustainability of the FWD Group. Strategic risks also address issues that involve the long-
term direction of the FWD Group.

Group risk

Group risk refers to risks arising from being a member of a group. This considers the risks of an event to a group
as a whole or to individual members which can adversely impact other members of the group. Group risk
considers the inter-relationships between members of the group including control, influence and
interdependence. As a group operating in 10 markets with more than 50 subsidiaries, every entity within the
Group is exposed to group risk.

The Group also maintains a central record to monitor intra-group transactions and other arrangements. The
central record is subject to continued review to ensure its accuracy and completeness, with a risk assessment
undertaken as part of the Group’s regular risk management process to identify material transactions and
implement suitable controls accordingly.

Channel risk

Channel or sales channel is the primary contact point between FWD Group and its customers or policyholders.
Channel risk is highly associated with the ability to attract and retain customers through product offerings. To
some extent, channel risk also deals with the quality and competitiveness of its contact with customers which
often leads to many related risks, particularly those related to compliance risk and operational risks.

Reputation risk

Reputation risk refers to risks arising from any potential negative perception from customers, regulators, or
counterparties regarding the FWD Group’s business practices, regulatory compliance, and current and
prospective financial status and/or solvency, including any indirect negative perception from its shareholders,
investors or major business partners that could impair its ability to maintain/establish its existing/new
relationships or services. Reputation risk could be caused by systemic or industry-wide factors in which FWD
Group operates. Reputation risk usually results from other risk issues and cannot be quantitatively assessed in
isolation. A Complaint Policy is in place to handle customer complaints. A Crisis and Business Continuity
Management Policy is in place to minimise the negative influence of a crisis event.

Business intelligence risk

Business intelligence risk refers to risks arising from a failure to adequately define, gather, analyse, and distribute
intelligence about products, customers, competitors, and any aspect of the environment needed to support
FWD Group executives and managers making strategic decisions. It is the organisational function’s responsibility
for the early identification of risks and opportunities in the market before they become obvious.

Technological strategy risk

Technological strategy risk refers to risks arising from a failure to leverage technology to provide solutions that
meet new requirements and market needs. This is accomplished through innovative products, processes,
services and technologies. FWD is exposed to the risk due to our strategy to create fresh customer experience
supported by leading digital technologies. However, the risk is not easily assessed nor quantified. The Group
keeps abreast of the development of technologies and customer needs and ensures adequate resources to
support relevant technological initiatives.

                    Risk management




Political and social risk

The risk FWD Group faces because of political and social changes or instability in a jurisdiction, country or
region.

Environmental and climate risk

Environmental risk refers to the risk posed by the exposure of the Company to activities that may potentially
cause or be affected by environmental degradation.

Climate risk refers to the risk posed by the exposure of the Company to physical, transition or liability risks
caused by or related to climate change.

Further details on our approach to managing environmental and climate-related risks and opportunities are set
out in the section titled “Building climate resilience in our business” in the section headed “Financial and
operating review — Environmental, social and governance” in this annual report.

Insurance risks
FWD Group is exposed to insurance risks as we provide protection and wealth management products and
services to customers. More specifically the risk exists where the actual experience is different from the
assumptions adopted when designing the products.

Indicators are monitored to assess the risk level, which include the actual to experience ratios and combined
ratios. To manage the risk, the Group also utilises several benchmarks to assess the pricing adequacy of a new
product and the ongoing appropriateness of an existing product. Where a product does not meet the internal
criteria, the product is subject to review.

We are also exposed to failure of reinsurers due to the reinsurance arrangements across Business Units.

Many insurance-related risk parameters are characterised by the following three risk components:

• volatility: The risk that the actual value differs from that expected, assuming the best-estimate parameter is
   true. Volatility is the result of the randomness of the risk process.

• catastrophe: The risk of a one-time claim of extreme proportions due to a certain major event, which is not
   caused by a change of parameters. The event can be viewed as a one-year shock. Examples of catastrophe
   risk are epidemics, earthquakes, floods and terrorist attacks.

• uncertainty: The risk of parameter estimation as a result of statistical estimation errors and changes of the
   parameter over time.
