 Overview      Financial and operating review   Corporate governance   Financial statements   Additional information

                     Risk management




Mortality risk

Mortality risk is associated with life expectancy. There are two types of mortality risk:

• higher than expected mortality risk: when more insured individuals die than expected, leading to higher
   claims (typical in traditional whole life, endowment and term products); and

• lower than expected mortality risk (longevity risk): when insured individuals live longer than expected,
   leading to higher claims (typical in pure endowment, annuity and pension products).

Mortality within one year (volatility and catastrophe) can impact the profitability of FWD Group in the year and
future cash flows. The uncertainty component of mortality assumptions may result in an increase in the liabilities,
which could adversely affect overall profitability.

Morbidity risk

Morbidity risk is associated with health events where FWD Group is exposed to indemnifying or reimbursing
losses caused by illness, accident or disability, or for expenses of medical treatment necessitated by illness,
accident or disability. Morbidity risk comprises of the risk of variability of size, frequency and time to payment of
future claims, development of outstanding claims and allocated loss adjustment expenses for morbidity product
lines over the remaining contract period.

Persistency risk

Persistency risk is the risk associated with adverse variations in persistency rates of policyholders from those in
the best estimate assumptions. In all life insurance business the policyholder has the (one-sided) option to end
the contract before the maturity date.

Expense risk

Expense risk is the risk that actual operational expenses in the future exceed the expected costs assumed in the
pricing assumptions.

Underwriting risk

Underwriting risk arises from evaluating, assessing and accepting business or risks (insurance policy application)
by underwriters which could result in poor or different portfolio behaviours to those assumed in the pricing and
reserving processes.

Claim risk

Claim risk is the risk that the claim payment exceeds the claim reserve due to poor claim assessment and claim
management, or payment is made to invalid claims, including fraudulent claims.

Pricing risk

The Company’s products usually have a very long maturity. Therefore, inadequate pricing of a product due to
inaccurate assumptions, model or other calculation error can expose the FWD Group to long-term problems,
such as loss, or capital inadequacy.

Model risk

The risk of adverse consequences (e.g. financial loss, poor decision making or damage to reputation) arising from
the improper design, development, implementation and/or use of a model. The risk can originate from, among
other things, incorrect parameter estimates; flawed hypotheses and/or assumptions; inaccurate, inappropriate
or incomplete data; and inadequate monitoring and/or controls.

                   Risk management




Compliance risks and operational risks
The risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failure in internal processes, people and systems or from external
events is defined as operational risk, including Compliance risk. To mitigate this risk, a comprehensive internal
control framework is implemented with responsibilities assigned across the Group’s Three Lines of Defence
governance structure.

Compliance risk is the risk of losses from damage to reputation, legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss or
loss of licence to operate which flow from failure or perceived failure to meet the Company’s compliance
obligations. Compliance obligations arise from mandatory requirements such as applicable laws and regulations
or voluntary commitments such as organisational and industry standards and codes, contractual relationships,
principles of good governance and community and ethical standards. Breaches of regulations can lead to
penalties ranging from fines to suspension of licence; thus the impact cannot be easily quantified. Risk appetite
has been set for compliance risk in which the Group has no appetite for the risk of regulatory intervention
resulting from breaches of law or regulation. Compliance risk includes but is not limited to AML, CTF, sanctions,
anti-bribery and corruption, and conduct risk.

People

The Group faces challenges in recruiting, developing and retaining quality staff under keen industry competition.
At the same time, FWD’s business plans create demand for experienced staff. The risk is qualitative in nature.
Human Resources of both Group Office and Business Units address the risk through reviewing employee benefits
(versus respective market), talent management plans and employee engagement events.

Fraud risk

Fraud risk is the risk of loss from deception or dishonesty of individuals (including our distributors, employees or
customers) to defraud, misappropriate property or circumvent regulations, the law or company policies.

Physical security and safety

Losses arising from damage to physical assets from accidents.

Business continuity

Losses arising from inability to recover due to business disruption or system failure.

Transaction processing & execution

Losses from failed transaction processing or process management due to relations with trade counterparties and
vendors.

Technology

Losses arising from technology failures, inadequacies or failure in the management of technology systems and
associated processes.

Conduct

Losses arising or adverse consequences due to conducting insurance business in a way that does not ensure the
fair treatment of customers, fair outcomes for customers, or which results in harm to customers (including mis-
selling).

Legal

Losses arising from legal proceedings due to contractual or intellectual property disputes. Non-compliance with
legislative requirements that lead to regulatory penalties or customer litigation.

Financial crime

Financial Crime Compliance risk refers to the loss from any offence involving handling money or property that is
from the proceeds of crimes or financing terrorism; the abuse of entrusted power for gain by offering (or
promising to offer) or receiving anything of value; failing to report the tax residence status; from any misconduct
in or misuse of information related to a financial market. The Group Anti-Money Laundering / Counter Terrorist
Financing and Sanctions Policy sets out the requirements of the Group AML/CTF programme, including a risk-
based approach to conducting customer due diligence, ongoing transaction monitoring, suspicious activity
reporting, training and record keeping.

                    Risk management




Regulatory compliance

Losses arising or adverse impact to business operations a from breach of regulation or industry practices and
codes, ineffective and non-transparent relationship with regulators or failure to effectively implement regulatory
changes.

Privacy

Loss arising from inappropriate management of personal data.

Third party

Losses from failed transaction processing or process management due to relations with outsourcing vendors or

Information security (including cyber)

Losses arising from failure to safeguard company and customer information.

Statutory reporting and tax

Losses arising from penalties due to failure to meet regulatory obligations in financial reporting or tax filings.

Data management

Losses arising from poor data management, inadequate data analysis, unavailability of data, poor data quality,
inadequate data architecture/IT infrastructure, inadequate data storage/retention and data destruction
management.

Model

Losses arising from errors in design, methodology, implementation or application. Failure to detect changes,
error inputs and outputs. Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect
or misused model outputs and reports. Model risk can lead to financial loss, poor business and strategic decision
making, or damage to reputation. The operational risk component includes misuse or errors in implementation,
model governance breaches, etc.

Investment, asset liability management & capital risks
As an insurance group, ALM risks are among the principal risks of FWD Group and are the key drivers of capital
requirements. FWD Group is exposed to market risk as the Business Units sell insurance and investment products
where liabilities are set up while assets backing liabilities are held. Since both assets and liabilities are sensitive
to interest rate movement, we are exposed to interest rate risk where there are mismatches.

FWD Group manages its assets and liabilities according to its ALM and market risk related policies, which
address risks arising from market exposures, asset-liability mismatches, liquidity management, currency
exposures and fund segregation. We manage our investments in accordance with our investment management
framework, which seeks to ensure that our investment functions are effective and compliant with relevant laws
and regulations. It also requires that our investment functions adhere to our ethical standards and risk
management policies.

Market risk

Market risk is defined as the risk of adverse changes in the value of its capital resources, due to unexpected
changes in the level or volatility of market prices of assets and liabilities, resulting from changes in, but not
limited to, interest rate levels, credit spreads, equity price levels and exchange rates. For further details of our
exposure to fluctuation in exchange rates and related hedges, please refer to note 28 to the consolidated
financial statements in this annual report.

Market risk cannot be eliminated through diversification, though it can be hedged in other ways and tends to
influence the entire market at the same time.

Counterparty risk

Counterparty risk is the risk that third parties fail to meet their obligations when they fall due. Although the
primary source of counterparty risk is the FWD Group’s investment portfolio, such risk can also arise through
reinsurance, procurement and treasury activities.

 Overview     Financial and operating review   Corporate governance      Financial statements    Additional information

                    Risk management




Liquidity risk

Liquidity risk occurs when FWD Group is unable to realise investments and other assets in order to settle its
financial obligations, including collateral needs, when they fall due. Liquidity risk is an asset and liability concern;
it is neither solely an asset nor a liability risk. Liquidity requirements may also have to be met under different
stress scenarios, such as a sudden increase in surrenders under a rising yield market resulting in unexpected
significant cash outflows from policyholders’ voluntary termination of their policy before its maturity.

Asset concentration risk

A concentrated position refers to the significant presence of a single security, securities of a single issuer or a
certain asset class or market segment relative to FWD Group’s overall portfolio. Concentrated positions prevent
diversification. A concentrated portfolio exposes FWD Group to the risks of portfolio underperformance,
portfolio volatility, reduction in income and capital loss if forced to exit at wrong time.

The greatest aggregate concentration of fair value to direct holding of an individual issuer (excluding all
government related fixed income assets) is less than 1 per cent of the total investments as at 31 December 2025.

Asset liability matching risk

ALM is the practice of managing risks that arise due to mismatches between the assets and liabilities of an
insurance company. A clearly defined ALM strategy should be articulated for each fund or segment and a
company and for the FWD Group as a whole. In most cases, the strategy will take the form of a target SAA that
sets out target allocations for each asset class.

The Group and its Business Units have specific ALM related goals and objectives, whilst these differ depending
upon their individual circumstances and environment, there are some overarching principles that are applied.
These principles ensure that any local legislation that may apply to the treatment of assets and liabilities is
considered and that asset cash flows are managed in relation to liability cash flows in a manner that is within the
agreed limits and risk appetite of the Group. Additionally, only asset classes permitted by FWD Group can be
invested in and any financial derivative instruments must never be used for speculative purposes.

Assets and liabilities are considered to be well matched if their changes in value in response to market
movements are highly correlated and within predefined risk metric limits. In assessing its acceptable asset-
liability mismatch, each Business Unit determines the appropriate metrics and respective risk thresholds and has
approvals for these from the Group or Business Unit ALM Committee. These typically include mismatches
between the asset and liability cashflows, duration, dollar duration, liquidity and currency.

The duration of interest-bearing financial assets is regularly reviewed and monitored by referencing the
estimated duration of insurance contract liabilities at segment-level.

In order to reduce exposure to changes in interest rates, the Group seeks to match, to the extent possible and
appropriate, the duration of assets and related liabilities. However, the availability of assets of suitable duration
may be restricted by applicable insurance laws, rules and regulations, market supply and other market factors.

Specific governance processes and procedures are in place for ALM to ensure any breaches or errors are
identified quickly and escalated.

Capital management risk

FWD aims to manage its business to ensure it maintains sufficient capital for the Group to support the GMCR,
GPCR and the Group Internal Economic Capital Assessment (GIECA) after a 1-in-20 stress event over a one year
time horizon, and sufficient funding is available to support the business activities and capital needs of operating
units, whilst creating sustainable value and earnings consistent with stakeholder’s expectations while achieving a
minimum of an investment grade credit rating for the Group.

Other risk exposures
Emerging risks

Emerging risks are risks which may develop or which already exist and are continuously evolving. As these risks
have often not emerged yet, data which would help to adequately assess the frequency and severity may not
even exist.


Intra-group transactions
The Group’s Business Units operate independently and, overall, there is limited interconnectedness across the
Group. Intra-group transactions are overseen by the relevant Group Office functions to ensure adherence with
the relevant Group policies. In this regard, the Group has adopted processes to identify and assess material
systematic intra-group transaction risks, ensuring that risks assumed are within the Group’s risk appetite. During
the year ended 31 December 2025, material intra-group transactions are related to reinsurance, intra-group
remittances, loans, recharges, funding and bonds. All intra-group transactions are non-complex and carried out
as part of the normal course of business for an insurance group.

In 2025, intra-group revenue for recharges, net remittances from operating subsidiaries, and intra-group
receivables/payable for recharges eliminations amounted to US$212 million, US$529 million and US$325 million
respectively (2024: US$172 million, US$589 million and US$283 million).

Corporate governance report
Corporate Governance Code – statement of compliance
The Company is listed on the main board of the Stock Exchange and, as required, has adopted a governance
structure based on the Corporate Governance Code. This corporate governance report explains how the
principles set out in the Corporate Governance Code have been applied.

Throughout the year ended 31 December 2025, except for Code Provision C.6.3, the Company complied with all
applicable code provisions in the Corporate Governance Code set out in Appendix C1 to the Listing Rules. Code
Provision C.6.3 provides that the company secretary should report to the chairman of the board and/or the chief
executive. The Company operates under a variant of this model whereby the Company Secretary reports to the
Group General Counsel, who is ultimately accountable for the company secretarial function of the Company and
who reports to our Group Chief Financial Officer, who in turn reports directly to the Group CEO.


Doing the Right Things Right at FWD
Besides our people, our reputation is our most important asset. Good governance protects both. That is why we
Do the Right Things Right. We have developed structures and processes that guide us daily as we identify,
manage and report risks. Our approach is driven by the same core values that drive everything else we do:
putting customers first, leveraging technology to drive innovation and empowering our people to deliver
sustainable growth.


Corporate governance framework
FWD defines corporate governance as “the structures, operating models, individuals and other mechanisms that
allow for robust management and control over the business operations, with due consideration to long-term
shareholder value and the interests of key stakeholders (including customers, regulators and other partners)”.

Effective corporate governance enables the Group to achieve its strategic objectives in accordance with its risk
philosophy and risk appetite. Our corporate governance framework is implemented across the Group, with
Business Units expected to align local practices with Group expectations and report any instances of non-
compliance in accordance with our robust escalation mechanisms.

The Board takes ultimate responsibility for the risk management activities of FWD Group. It is responsible for
reviewing and approving our strategies, plans, policies and risk appetite. It therefore plays a critical role in
ensuring sound and prudent policies and practices are in-effect for ensuring good governance – and has
continuous oversight of risk management, internal controls and compliance matters.

Non-executive Directors




Independent Non-executive Directors




The Board is currently made up of 13 Directors, of which two are Executive Directors (including the Group CEO),
two are Non-executive Directors and nine are Independent Non-executive Directors (including the Chairman).
The number of Independent Non-executive Directors represents more than one-third of the Board as required by
Rule 3.10A of the Listing Rules. Biographies of our Directors are in the section headed “Corporate governance —
Board of Directors” in this annual report.

The Directors are not appointed for a specific term. However, all Directors are subject to retirement by rotation
at least once every three years and are eligible for re-election at the general meetings of the Company in
accordance with the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company.

Roles and responsibilities of the Board and senior management
The Board is ultimately responsible for directing the Group as a going concern and is collectively responsible to
the Shareholders for the long-term success of the Group. Their roles and responsibilities include (either by itself
or through delegation to the Audit Committee, Risk Committee, Compensation Committee and Nomination
Committee):

• formulating the long-term strategy of the Group, and monitoring the implementation of its strategic
      objectives with appropriate focus on value creation and risk management;

• monitoring the Group’s operating and financial performance;
• ensuring that effective governance and sound risk management and internal control systems are in place;
• shaping and monitoring the Group’s culture;
• leading, directing and supervising the Company’s affairs to enable the long term success of the Company;
• setting long-term strategic objectives and strategic policies;
• ensuring appropriate and adequate reporting in the annual reports, including financial statements, ESG,
      disclosures of the Board’s practices (e.g., the terms of references of its committees), and various policies
      (e.g., shareholder communication, remuneration, nomination, dividend and diversity policies);

• being accountable – the Directors should be held accountable for their actions or inactions and, where
      appropriate, take the Shareholders’ interests into account in their decisions;

• ensuring adequacy of resources, qualifications and experience, especially for the Group’s accounting,
      internal audit and financial reporting functions; and


130 FWD Group Holdings Limited Annual Report 2025
 Overview     Financial and operating review     Corporate governance       Financial statements     Additional information

                                                 Corporate governance
                                                        report



• ensuring the fullest communication with Shareholders and the Company’s recognition of their interest.
The Board delegates authority to the Group CEO who further delegates authority to members of senior
management responsible for carrying out the day-to-day operations of the Group in line with the Group’s overall
strategy and within the confines of policies set by the Board. Senior management is also responsible for ensuring
the Board remains appraised of matters through providing adequate and timely reporting for its consideration.
Senior management is accountable for ensuring day-to-day business operations and related activities are
performed in accordance with all relevant internal and external expectations, including that risk taking is aligned
with risk appetite. Individuals with the appropriate skills, experiences and credentials are appointed to senior
management roles.

The Company has adopted with effect from 7 July 2025, the date on which the Company was listed on the Stock
Exchange (Listing Date), its own FWD Group Directors/Chief Executives Dealing and Disclosure Policy on terms
no less exacting than those set out in the Model Code. All of the Directors (including the Group CEO) have
confirmed, following specific enquiry by the Company, that they have complied with the required standards set
out in the FWD Group Directors/Chief Executives Dealing and Disclosure Policy from the Listing Date.


Diversity
Diversity of the Board
FWD is committed to building a diverse, equitable, inclusive and collaborative culture. We recognise and
embrace the importance of having a diverse Board, which we believe is an essential element in maintaining an
effective Board and contributing to the sustainable development of the Group. Our Board Diversity Policy aims
to enhance the Board’s effectiveness and corporate governance standards of the Group through promoting and
achieving diversity on the Board.

We believe that the Board members should represent a diversity of perspectives and experiences, which can be
achieved through a number of factors, including, but not limited to: professional experience, skills, expertise,
knowledge, independence, composition (including gender identity, age, disability, race, ethnicity, sexual
orientation, education and cultural background), tenure on the Board and other factors relevant and applicable
to achieving a diverse Board, as well as to the effectiveness of the Board and requirements of our business from
time to time.

The following diagram illustrates the diversity profile of the Board:

Independence                             Executive                 Non-executive                   Independent Non-
                                                                                                       executive
                                         2 directors                    2 directors                    9 directors
Age Group                                  40-54                          55-69                           Over 70
                                         3 directors                    6 directors                   4 directors
Gender                                             Female                                          Male
                                                4 directors                                    9 directors

The Board at a minimum ensures that there is not a single gender Board. The Board also ensures that the
Nomination Committee includes at least one Director of a different gender. Currently, there are three female
members of the Nomination Committee and we are committed to maintaining more than the minimum required
levels for female representation on the Board and its committees.

The Nomination Committee is responsible for reviewing the structure, size and composition of the Board,
selecting the individuals to be nominated as Directors, reviewing and monitoring the implementation of our
Group Board Diversity Policy and ensuring our Board Diversity Policy is implemented in an effective and practical
manner, reviewing the succession plan of Directors and making recommendations on these matters to the Board
for approval. This helps ensure that the Board has a balanced composition of skills, experience, expertise,
independence and knowledge appropriate to the requirements of the businesses of FWD, with due regard for
the benefits of diversity on the Board.

The Nomination Committee has reviewed the implementation of the Board Diversity Policy for the year ended 31
December 2025 and is satisfied with the current level of the Board’s diversity having considered, amongst other
factors, the current skills matrix of the Board (as set out on page 130) and the diversity profile of the Board (as set
out above).

Workforce diversity
For employees of the Group, there is a separate diversity, equity and inclusion strategy.

The Group adopted the FWD Group Workplace Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DEI) Policy, as we are committed to
fostering a diverse, equitable, and inclusive workplace, recognising that diversity of talent, experience, and
perspective is essential to the Group’s long-term success and innovation. The policy applies to all employees and
contractors across all functions and locations.

The policy affirms the Group’s commitment to:

• providing equal opportunities in recruitment, development, and promotion based on merit and potential;
• creating a respectful, inclusive, and psychologically safe work environment;
• preventing and addressing all forms of discrimination, harassment, and bias, with zero tolerance for
   retaliation; and

• ensuring decision-makers receive unconscious bias training.
The Company values diversity in all its forms, including but not limited to gender, age, ethnicity, cultural
background, nationality, disability, sexual orientation, religion, marital or family status, educational and
professional background, and life experiences.

Implementation of the policy is overseen by Group Human Resources, with managers and leaders expected to
model inclusive behaviours and all personnel encouraged to participate in DEI initiatives. Regular training and
awareness sessions are provided, and concerns can be reported confidentially through designated channels,
with all reports handled promptly and fairly.

Progress on DEI is monitored through dashboards and employee feedback, and the policy will be reviewed at
least annually by the Nomination Committee to ensure alignment with best practices, legal requirements, and
the Group’s strategic goals.

As at 31 December 2025, 54 per cent of the workforce are female. Women made up 33 per cent of our assistant
vice presidents or above.


Appointment and re-election of Directors
The Company has put in place a formal and transparent process for the appointment of Directors. The
Nomination Committee is responsible for identifying and nominating suitable candidates. Further details on the
work of the Nomination Committee can be found in this corporate governance report.

The Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company provide that any Director appointed to fill a
casual vacancy or as an addition to the existing Board shall hold office only until the first annual general meeting
of the Company after his/her appointment and be subject to re-election at such general meeting.

In addition, under the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company, at each annual general
meeting, one-third of the Directors for the time being, or if their number is not three or a multiple of three, the
number nearest to but not less than one-third, shall retire from office by rotation, provided that every Director
shall be subject to retirement by rotation at least once every three years. Any Director who has not been subject
to retirement by rotation in the three years preceding the annual general meeting shall retire by rotation at such
annual general meeting. Any further Directors so to retire shall be those who have been longest in office since
their last re-election or appointment and so that as between persons who became or were last re-elected
Directors on the same day those to retire shall (unless they otherwise agree among themselves) be determined
by lot. A retiring Director shall be eligible for re-election.


Independence of the Board
Nine members of the Board (approximately 69 per cent) are Independent Non-executive Directors and they met
the independence guidelines set out in Rule 3.13 of the Listing Rules. The Nomination Committee reviews the
independence of Independent Non-executive Directors annually. None of the Independent Non-executive
Directors have any business with or significant financial interests in the Company or its subsidiaries. Therefore,
the Board considers all the Independent Non-executive Directors to be independent. The Independent Non-
executive Directors constitute a majority of the Board and provide appropriate challenge and views for the


132 FWD Group Holdings Limited Annual Report 2025
 Overview     Financial and operating review   Corporate governance    Financial statements   Additional information

                                               Corporate governance
                                                      report



benefit of the Board as a whole. Directors are entitled to request further information from management and
obtain, at the Company’s expense, external independent professional advice if and when necessary. Therefore,
there is a strong element of independence on the Board and independent views and inputs are available to
ensure effective operations of the Board.

Board Succession
The Company recognises the importance of board succession planning in maintaining long-term corporate
stability, ensuring continuity of leadership, and supporting the execution of its strategic objectives. A sound
succession framework also helps minimise operational risks arising from Board turnover while enabling the Board
to optimise its overall composition, diversity, and skill sets.

The Board, through the Nomination Committee, regularly reviews the composition and skills matrix of the Board,
conducts an annual formal assessment of the Board’s performance, and will make any recommendations on
proposed changes to the Board. The Company is satisfied that the Board currently possesses an appropriate
balance of skills, perspectives and experience, background, gender, and tenure. Further, the Board maintains a
strong element of independence, as discussed in the section headed “Independence of the Board” in this
corporate governance report.
As the Company was newly listed in July 2025, the tenure of each Director is less than one year as measured
from the Listing Date. The Board therefore expects that its overall composition will remain relatively stable in the
near term. Nevertheless, the Board remains open to considering prospective candidates for directorships as the
Company evolves. Appointments will be based on the factors set out in the Board Diversity Policy and
Nomination Policy, including but not limited to integrity, experience, skills and diversity. The Board may engage
external advisors to support in the search for directors.


Evaluation of the Board
The Board undertakes a formal assessment of its own and its committees’ performance annually to assess their
effectiveness in discharging their respective roles and responsibilities, and to identify areas and opportunities for
enhancements or improvements. The evaluation in 2025 was undertaken through the following activities for the
review period from the fourth quarter of 2024 to the third quarter of 2025:

• conducting a review led by Professor MA Si Hang, Frederick by way of a tailored self-assessment
   questionnaire covering a comprehensive range of topics including the Board’s composition and skills, Board
   processes, culture and dynamics, quality and timeliness of information received, compliance and training, risk
   management and internal controls, and stakeholder engagement; and

• review of relevant governance documentation, such as the Board and its committee meeting agendas,
   minutes, reports and associated processes.

The assessment criteria used in the Board’s effectiveness review are aligned with the assessment criteria set out
in the HKEX Corporate Governance Guide for Boards and Directors for Board performance review.
The overall assessment concluded the Board was generally effective during the review period and identified
various areas of particular strength and areas of focus to further enhance the overall effectiveness of the Board.
The Board evaluation has helped us to formulate actions to facilitate greater interactions between the Board
members and senior management (including senior management within our Business Units), as well as to
enhance the Board processes, timely provision of information, and governance practices.

Committee functions
The Audit Committee had six members as at 31 December 2025, including five Independent Non-executive
Directors and one Non-executive Director. Mr. Andrew WEIR serves as Chairman of the Audit Committee and
has the appropriate accounting or related financial management expertise. Three members of the Audit
Committee constitute a quorum for the transaction of business and the act of a majority of those present at any
meeting at which there is a quorum qualifies as an act of the Audit Committee.

The Audit Committee has delegated authority from the Board to independently review the effectiveness of the
Group’s financial reporting processes, risk management and internal control systems.

The Audit Committee mandate includes:

• overseeing the integrity of the Group’s accounts, financial statements and reports and other financial
    disclosures, reviewing annual, semi-annual and any quarterly results, reviewing significant financial reporting
    judgements contained within and any significant financial reporting issues identified;

• reviewing the adequacy and effectiveness of the Group’s risk management, budgetary and financial control
    and internal control systems;

• reviewing and approving the Group’s internal audit charter, three year audit workplan and ensuring that
    adequate resources are provided to carry out the Group’s internal audit activities effectively; and

• making recommendations in relation to the appointment, re-appointment, resignation and removal of the
    external auditor, and approving the external auditor’s remuneration and terms of engagement.

Key activities during the year
• monitoring the integrity of the Group’s accounts, financial statements and reports, and reviewing significant
    financial reporting judgements contained in them;

• reviewing and approving, and making recommendations to the Board in respect of, the draft preliminary
    results announcement, interim report, consolidated financial statements and supplementary embedded value
    information of the Company for the six months ended 30 June 2025;

• reviewing the external auditor’s management letter, any material queries raised by the auditor to
    management in respect of the accounting records, financial accounts or systems of control and
    management’s response;

• oversight over internal control system;
• reviewing and approving the annual internal audit charter and three-year internal audit work plan;
• discussing the results of work and reported findings of the Group’s internal audit;

The Nomination Committee has delegated authority from the Board to identify and nominate suitable candidates
to become Directors and senior management of the Group to take a leadership role in shaping the corporate
governance of the Company and overseeing the Company’s ESG and sustainability strategy, initiatives, policies
and performance.

The Nomination Committee mandate includes:

• reviewing the structure, size and composition (including the balance of skills, knowledge and experience and

   other factors which are relevant to the Company;

• supporting the Board in overseeing the evaluation of the Board;
• making recommendations to the Board on the appointment or re-appointment of Directors and succession
   planning for Directors;

Nomination Policy
The Board has adopted the Nomination Policy with effect from the Listing Date which sets out the procedures
and key criteria to be used by the Nomination Committee for the selection, appointment and re-appointment of
directors, the senior management and key persons in control functions.

The Company has put in place a formal and transparent process for the appointment of Directors. When a need
is identified, the Nomination Committee engages in a robust search process to identify suitably qualified
Director candidates. Prospective candidates will then be shortlisted through a comprehensive evaluation process
that includes consideration of a candidate’s ability and willingness to devote sufficient time to the duties
required. The Nomination Committee will consider the candidates for directorship, and make nominations to the
Board for consideration and approval, and recommendation. The key factors considered in assessing the
suitability of a proposed candidate for directorship are as follows:

• reputation for integrity;
• accomplishment, expertise and experience in the financial services industry, in particular the insurance
   sector;

• commitment in respect of available time and relevant interest, in particular, whether he/she would be able to
   devote sufficient time and attention to the Board;

• how the proposed candidate’s skills fit into the current mix of skills of the Board;
• in the case of an Independent Non-executive Director, criteria of independence as prescribed under the
   Listing Rules and the Guideline on Group Supervision issued by IA from time to time; and

• diversity in all aspects, including but not limited to gender, age, cultural and educational background,
   ethnicity, professional experience, skills, knowledge and length of service.

Key activities during the year
• supporting the Board in reviewing the effectiveness of the Board and its committees;
• reviewing and making recommendations to the Board to approve the revised terms of reference of the
   Nomination Committee and the Nomination Policy;

• recommending changes to the compositions of the Board and its committees;
• reviewing the Company’s compliance with the Corporate Governance Code;
• overseeing the programme of continuing training and development for the Board;
• approval of annual assessment proposal and process for implementation on each individual director’s time
   commitment and contribution;

• approval of the proposal for investment portfolio climate action plan; and
• approval of the Group’s ESG materiality assessment and the Scope 3 - Financed Emissions Disclosure in the
   section headed “Financial & operating review — Environmental, social and governance — Sustainable
   investment” in this annual report.

Risk management and internal controls
The Board, supported by the Audit Committee and Risk Committee, is responsible for overseeing the risk
management and internal control systems of the Group. Through its regular review of these systems, the Board
covers all material controls, including financial, operational and compliance controls.

The Group has established risk management and internal control systems consisting of organisational
frameworks, policies, procedures and risk management methods which the Board and management believe are
appropriate for the Group’s business operations. The Group continues to invest in these systems to improve
them, and to undertake initiatives and measures to address the potential weaknesses in these systems. The
Group’s ERM framework and internal control systems are designed to manage rather than eliminate risks and can
only provide reasonable and not absolute assurance against material misstatement or loss as they are designed
to mitigate rather than eliminate the risk of failure to achieve business objectives, and have inherent limitations.
The effectiveness of the Group’s risk management and internal control systems depends on their regular
maintenance, upgrades and updates, so that they can handle the expansion in information as the Group expands
its existing operations, as well as proper implementation and integration by the Group’s employees. The main
features of the ERM framework and the process to identify, evaluate and manage risks are set out in the section
headed “Financial and operating review — Risk management” in this annual report.




142 FWD Group Holdings Limited Annual Report 2025
 Overview     Financial and operating review   Corporate governance     Financial statements   Additional information

                                               Corporate governance
                                                      report



FWD’s internal control system is the primary means by which the Group mitigates inherent risk exposures to
yield a residual and expected risk exposure that is aligned with its risk appetite. In particular, an Operational Risk
Management and Internal Controls Policy is in place to ensure that the key controls within key business
processes are subject to regular review by key process owners and the Risk Management function. The Group
has an internal audit function, which performs independent assessment of the design and operating
effectiveness of the internal control system and reports results to the Audit Committee.

The Board, through the Audit Committee and the Risk Committee, reviews the effectiveness of risk management
and internal controls annually, in particular, the relevant committee reviews:

• the adequacy of resources in the internal audit function, including skills and capabilities to perform its duties;
• the scope of work performed by both internal and external auditors and outcomes of internal and external
   audits, related to internal controls;

• areas of risk identified by management as well as the scope and quality of ongoing risk and internal control
   monitoring, carried out by management, and the communication of monitoring results;

• the quality and scope of the internal control system implemented by management and the work and
   effectiveness of the internal audit function as well as any significant risks reported by the internal audit
   function;

• the changes in the nature and extent of risks, and the Group’s ability to respond to changes in its business
   and the external environment;

• whether significant control failings or weaknesses have been identified during the year, their potential impact
   on the Group and remedial actions;

• the annual report on ORSA;
• the effectiveness of processes in the area of financial reporting and compliance with regulatory requirements;
   and

• the results of management’s internal control self-assessment exercises.
The annual review of the Group’s risk management and internal control systems was conducted by an internal
risk management and internal control systems certification process performed by management, supported by
the internal audit function which performed an independent assessment on the appropriateness and
effectiveness of the internal control environment.

During the reporting period, there were no significant changes in the assessment of risks (including ESG risks)
and the risk management and internal control systems.

Management has confirmed to the Board that the Group’s risk management and internal control systems are
appropriate and effective. Based on the review result and management’s confirmation, the Board considered the
Group’s risk management and internal control systems to be appropriate and effective for the year ended 31
December 2025.

Inside information
The Company has implemented procedures and internal controls concerning the safeguarding and dissemination
of inside information as follows:

• the Company’s Group Communications Policy has established a control process for the management of
   communications with various internal and external stakeholders. Named spokespersons are authorised to
   provide information about the Group to relevant stakeholders;

• the Company has established the Inside Information Disclosure Policy to ensure appropriate handling of
   inside information and that any required disclosure of inside information is made in a manner that provides
   for equal, timely and effective access by market participants and the public to the information disclosed. The
   policy has been communicated to all relevant staff and related training has also been provided to them; and

• the Company’s Code of Ethics and Business Conduct prohibits the unauthorised use of confidential or non-
   public information.

Dividends
The Company has adopted a dividend policy which sets out the principles and guidelines that the Company
intends to apply in relation to the declaration, payment, or distribution of its profits as dividends to Shareholders.
In considering the payment of dividends, the Board seeks to balance retaining adequate reserves for maintaining
working capital and supporting future growth, with allowing Shareholders to participate in the Company’s
profits.

When considering the recommendation or payment of dividends and determining the dividend amount, the
Board will take into account, among other factors:

• the actual and expected financial performance of the Group;
• the Group’s expected working capital (including Group solvency) requirements, capital expenditure
   requirements and future expansion plans;

• the amount of retained earnings and distributable reserves of the Company and each of the members of the
   Group, and the distributions received by the Company from its subsidiaries;

• the Group’s cash flow and liquidity position;
• prevailing economic and market conditions, business cycle of the Group’s business and other internal or
   external factors that may have an impact on the business or financial performance and position of the Group;
   and

• any other factors that the Board may consider relevant and appropriate.
The Company does not have any pre-determined dividend distribution ratio. As at the date of this annual report,
the Company has not declared or made any dividend or other distribution to its shareholders. As disclosed in the
Prospectus, the Company does not have any present plan to declare or pay any dividends on its ordinary shares
in the foreseeable future. The Group currently intends to retain most, if not all, of available funds and any future
earnings to operate and expand the business. Any other future determination to pay dividends will be made at
the discretion of the Board and subject to our constitutional documents and applicable laws and regulations.

If the Board decides to pay dividends, the form, frequency and amount may be based on a number of factors,
including the Group’s future operations and earnings, capital requirements and surplus, general financial
condition, contractual restrictions and other factors that the Board may deem relevant.

B. PineBridge and its subsidiaries (collectively, the PineBridge Group)

The PineBridge Group was indirectly majority owned and controlled by Mr. LI Tzar Kai, Richard. On 23
December 2024, MetLife Investment Management announced it had entered into an agreement to acquire the
PineBridge Group (excluding its private funds group business and joint venture in Mainland China) from PCG
(PineBridge Disposal). The transaction completed on 30 December 2025. Accordingly, members of the
PineBridge Group (excluding its private funds group business and joint venture in Mainland China) were
associates of Mr. LI Tzar Kai, Richard and thus connected persons of the Company under Chapter 14A of the
Listing Rules, but ceased to be so upon completion of the PineBridge Disposal.

As stated in the Prospectus, on 18 June 2025, a member of the Group and a member of the PineBridge Group
entered into a framework agreement (PineBridge Asset Management and Investment Services Agreement),
pursuant to which the member of the PineBridge Group will provide or grant, or procure other members of the
PineBridge Group to provide or grant, asset management and investment services to the Group. Such services
include, without limitation, investment management services and investment advisory services (PineBridge
Transaction).

The PineBridge Asset Management and Investment Services Agreement has a term of less than three years
commencing from the Listing Date and has been terminated with effect from 6 January 2026 after completion of
the PineBridge Disposal.

The management fees payable by the Group for the investment management services were generally
determined based on (i) an agreed fee rate calculated in relation to the net asset value and/or performance of,
and/or capital committed to, the relevant investment portfolio; (ii) a banded sliding scale of fee rates based on
the net asset value of the portfolio; or (iii) a fixed sum. The fees had been determined by reference to prevailing/
market rates, and are no less favourable to the Group than those offered by independent third parties/based on
similar contracts with similar third parties. In relation to the investment management services provided to FWD
Life Japan, the management fees were also determined after an arm’s length rule assessment. The management
fees payable by the Group for the investment advisory services were agreed by the relevant Group entity and the
relevant PineBridge entity.

The Group had followed the pricing policies as set out in the Prospectus when determining the price and terms
of the PineBridge Transaction.

D. Confirmations from the Directors, Independent Non-executive Directors and auditor of the Company

The Board, including the Independent Non-executive Directors, has reviewed and confirmed that the above
continuing connected transactions and other fully exempt continuing connected transactions during the year
ended 31 December 2025 were entered into:

(i) in the ordinary and usual course of business of the Group;

(ii) on normal commercial terms or better; and

(iii) according to the relevant agreements governing them on terms that are fair and reasonable and in the
interests of the Shareholders of the Company as a whole.

The Company’s auditor was engaged to report on the PCCW/HKT Transactions, the PineBridge Transaction and
the bolttech Transaction entered into by the Group during the year ended 31 December 2025 in accordance with
Hong Kong Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised) “Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or
Reviews of Historical Financial Information” and with reference to Practice Note 740 (Revised) “Auditor’s Letter
on Continuing Connected Transactions under the Hong Kong Listing Rules” issued by the Hong Kong Institute of
Certified Public Accountants. The auditor has confirmed in a letter to the Board that, with respect to the PCCW/
HKT Transactions, the PineBridge Transaction and the bolttech Transaction:

(i) nothing has come to the auditor’s attention that causes the auditor to believe that the disclosed continuing
connected transactions have not been approved by the Board;

(ii) for transactions involving the provision of goods or services by the Group, nothing has come to the auditor’s
attention that causes the auditor to believe that the transactions were not, in all material respects, in accordance
with the pricing policies of the Group;

(iii) nothing has come to the auditor’s attention that causes the auditor to believe that the transactions were not
entered into, in all material respects, in accordance with the relevant agreements governing such transactions;

the auditor’s attention that causes the auditor to believe that the disclosed continuing connected transactions
have exceeded the annual cap as set by the Company.

Use of proceeds
On 7 July 2025, in connection with the completion of our IPO, 91,342,100 Shares of US$0.03 each were issued at
an offer price of HK$38.00 per Share for a total cash consideration, before listing expenses, of approximately
HK$3,471 million (equivalent to approximately US$442 million).

On 1 August 2025, the Over-allotment Option described in the Prospectus was partially exercised by the Joint
Global Coordinators (for themselves and on behalf of the International Underwriters) in respect of an aggregate
of 5,001,400 Shares. After deducting the underwriting fees and commissions and expenses payable by the
Company, the net proceeds received by the Company from the IPO after the partial exercise of the Over-
allotment Option amounted to approximately HK$3,597 million (equivalent to approximately US$458 million).

The net proceeds from the IPO were utilised for our deleveraging and refinancing activities. This included
US$500 million deleveraging via the refinancing of the US$900 million Subordinated Notes due 2029,
redemption of the US$750 million Perpetual Capital Securities and the issuance of US$1.15 billion of
subordinated dated capital securities split between 5-year and 10-year tranches.

Remuneration governance
Role of the Compensation Committee
The main role of the Compensation Committee is to assist and advise the Board on the remuneration of the
Board and all employees of the FWD Group including senior management. In so doing, the Compensation
Committee has a formulated strategy and remuneration policies to cover all Directors and employees, as well as
a set of formal and transparent procedures to implement the policies. The key objective is to ensure that the
total remuneration packages we offer enable us to attract, motivate and retain highly talented individuals that
our business needs, and who enable the future success of FWD Group.

The Compensation Committee oversees the implementation of appropriate remuneration practices across the
Group. This includes:

• oversight of remuneration policies and remuneration practices aligned with the corporate culture, business
   objectives, risk appetite and long-term interests of the Group and its stakeholders;

• appropriateness of remuneration for all staff including senior management considering both performance and
   risk management;

• suitability of compensation payable to senior management for any loss or termination of office in accordance
   with contractual terms; and

• appropriateness of the compensation of the Directors, including the remuneration of the Chairman of the
   Board as well as indemnification and insurance matters.

Remuneration framework
Group Remuneration Policy
The remuneration of our employees is designed to provide equitable and competitive incentives to align with
shareholders’ interests and foster the long-term sustainable growth of the business within the overall risk
management framework. The remuneration mainly comprises base salary, allowance, short-term incentives and
long-term incentives. The variable remuneration component is linked to achievement of certain key performance
indicators. The table below summarises the remuneration elements for 2025.

Variable remuneration
Variable remuneration opportunities are designed to motivate employees to deliver on key short-term and long-
term objectives. The variable remuneration is linked to achievement of certain key performance indicators, with
the respective weightings reflecting our business strategies with a focus on sustainable and value-focused
growth. Depending on business and individual performance results, such incentives may result in award levels
above or below target, reflecting superior performance and performance below expectations, respectively.

Short-term incentive plan
Our short-term incentive plan recognises the contribution of all permanent employees to FWD’s short-term
success and incentivises the achievement of specific annual performance objectives that are aligned to our
strategy. It also provides a means to reward the individual and collective performance of our employees.

For 2025, the performance measures used in the short-term incentive plan were as follows1:

    Performance Measures                       Weighting           Description

    NB CSM                                         50%             NB CSM is a main growth driver for our Group




    OPAT2                                          15%             OPAT is based on the reported financial results as disclosed in the
                                                                   financial statements and is a key profitability metric



    NPAT2                                          15%             NPAT is based on the reported financial results as disclosed in the
                                                                   financial statements under IFRS accounting standards and is a key
                                                                   profitability metric


    Operating expenses /                           10%             Key expense management metric to achieve improvement in
    expense overrun                                                operating leverage and cost management

Long-term incentive plan
We offer a long-term incentive plan to senior employees of the FWD Group in order to recognise our people who
can influence, and contribute towards, the achievement of FWD’s long-term goals and success and to drive
retention of key talent.

There are two components to the long-term incentive plan:

    •   restricted share units (RSUs) which vest over three or four years. These are primarily designed as an
        employee retention tool; and

    •   performance share units (PSUs), which vest over three years, and are dependent on business
        performance. The performance factor applied to the PSUs serves as a multiplier on the number of PSUs
        originally granted and calculated at the end of the three-year vesting window.

The performance factor for 2025 long-term incentive plan is based on the following components:

 Performance Measures                          Description

 NPAT                                          Cumulative net profit after tax over the three years’ performance period as
                                               reported in the financial statements to drive a path to profitability growth
                                               and increase in shareholder value


 Total Shareholder Return (Absolute)           Total shareholder return (TSR) is the compound annual return from the
                                               ownership of a share over the performance period measured by calculating
                                               the change in share price and where applicable, gross value of dividends
                                               received (and reinvested), during the period


 Total Shareholder Return (Relative)           TSR is compared with the TSR of peer companies over the performance
                                               period. The peer group for the 2025 LTI include AIA, Prudential plc and
                                               Hang Seng Index

Additional information regarding share schemes
Equity Incentive Plans
The Group has three Equity Incentive Plans, namely:

(a) the FWD Share Option and RSU Plan (Share Option and RSU Plan);
(b) the FWD Share Award Plan (Share Award Plan); and
(c) the FWD Employee Share Purchase Plan (Employee Share Purchase Plan).

Share Option and RSU Plan
The Share Option and RSU Plan was jointly adopted by the boards of directors of FL and FGL on 28 November
2017 and was subsequently amended on 5 December 2018 and 30 January 2022. The terms of the Share Option
and RSU Plan are not subject to the provisions of Chapter 17 of the Listing Rules as the Group does not intend to
make any further grants of awards under the Share Option and RSU Plan after the Listing. The Board approved
the assumption of the outstanding awards by the Company on 16 August 2021 and 23 June 2022.

A summary of the key terms of the Share Option and RSU Plan is as follows:

(a) Purpose: The purpose of the Share Option and RSU Plan is to provide the Group with a flexible means to
retain, incentivise, reward, remunerate, compensate and/or provide benefits to its “eligible employees” (as
defined below).

(b) Participants: “Eligible employees” generally include any employee, consultant or director holding salaried
office or employment with (i) the Group; (ii) any entity over which the Group has “significant influence”; or (iii)
Mr. Li and all entities and persons that are subject to the “control” of Mr. Li.
(c) Maximum number of Shares available for issue: The maximum aggregate number of FL and FGL shares with
respect to which awards may be granted pursuant to the Share Option and RSU Plan was 2,000,000 FL shares
and 2,000,000 FGL shares (subject to adjustment) prior to the Listing and the assumption of the Pre-IPO Awards
by the Company (including as at 1 January 2025). However, as the Pre-IPO Awards granted pursuant to the Share
Option and RSU Plan that were outstanding as at the Listing will be satisfied by the Company on or after the
Listing, such limits in respect of FL and FGL shares are no longer relevant. The maximum total number of Shares
which may be issued upon vesting of all such outstanding Pre-IPO Awards granted pursuant to the Share Option
and RSU Plan represent, in aggregate, up to 25,410,704 Shares (i.e. approximately 1.99 per cent of Shares in issue
(excluding treasury shares) as at 31 December 2025).
(d) Maximum entitlement of each participant under the Share Option and RSU Plan: As disclosed above, the
Group does not intend to make any further grants of awards under the Share Option and RSU Plan after the
Listing. The maximum entitlement of each participant under the Share Option and RSU Plan, as far as Shares are
concerned, is limited to the Pre-IPO Awards that were outstanding as at the Listing Date.

(e) Exercise period and exercise price: For the reasons disclosed in note (6) to the table below, exercise period
and exercise price were no longer relevant with effect from the Listing Date.

(f) Vesting of awards: An award (or the relevant part thereof) will vest on the date or dates specified in the letter
of grant. An award (or the relevant part thereof) will not vest unless and until all applicable conditions to which it
is subject have been satisfied. An award may vest in full or in part, or an award may not vest, according to the
terms and conditions of the letter of grant. Such terms and conditions may include restrictions against disposal
of Shares that are or will be delivered upon vesting of the award, for a period after the vesting date.

(g) Amounts payable on application or acceptance of award: No consideration shall be payable by the
participant on acceptance of any RSUs or PSUs granted.

of the Share Option and RSU Plan, its terms shall remain in full force and effect in respect of RSUs and options
which have been awarded and which remain unvested or unexercised immediately prior to the termination. No
further awards will be granted under this plan after the Listing.

on 27 February 2023 with further minor amendments made on 8 August 2024 and 16 May 2025, in each case to
incorporate the requirements set out in the revised Chapter 17 of the Listing Rules which took effect from 1
January 2023. The Share Award Plan operates both before and after the Listing. The terms of the Share Award
Plan rules that are expressed to apply prior to the Listing are not subject to the provisions of Chapter 17 of the
Listing Rules. The terms of the Share Award Plan rules that are expressed to apply after the Listing are subject to
the provisions of Chapter 17 of the Listing Rules.

A summary of the key terms of the Share Award Plan is as follows:



                                                                                                                                                         171
 Overview     Financial and operating review   Corporate governance    Financial statements   Additional information

                                               Remuneration report




(a) Purpose: The purpose of the Share Award Plan is to provide the Company with a flexible means to retain,
incentivise, reward, remunerate and/or compensate its “eligible persons” (as defined below) by granting awards
in the form of RSUs, PSUs and/or options and drive the performance and growth of the Group's business by
providing such eligible persons with the opportunity to acquire equity interests in the Company.

(b) Participants: “Eligible persons” generally include (i) employees or directors employed or engaged by a
member of the Group; (ii) employees or directors employed or engaged by a “related entity”; (iii) (in respect of
One-Off Awards (as defined in the Prospectus) only granted prior to the Listing) employees or directors
employed by Mr. Li and entities under his “control”; and (iv) individual consultants, independent contractors, or
self-employed contractors who provide services to the Group on a continuing and recurring basis in its ordinary
and usual course of business which are in the interests of the long-term growth of the Group (excluding any non-
executive Directors, directors of the Group and any professional service providers who provide assurance or are
required to perform their services with impartiality and objectivity).
(c) Maximum number of Shares available for issue: After the Listing, the maximum aggregate number of new
Shares in respect of which awards may be granted is calculated as: X = A - B - C, where A = Plan Mandate Limit,
B = new Shares for awards already granted under the Share Award Plan, and C = new Shares for awards under
other share-based incentive plans. The Plan Mandate Limit may be renewed every three years subject to
Shareholders' approval.

(d) Maximum entitlement of each participant under the Share Award Plan: In any 12 month period, the maximum
number of new Shares issued and/or transferred (and to be issued and/or transferred) upon the vesting and/or
exercise of awards granted pursuant to the Share Award Plan and any other share-based incentive plans of the
Company to any participant shall not exceed 1% of the Shares in issue for the time being.

(e) Exercise period and exercise price: Any award of options which has vested, satisfied all conditions, and has
not lapsed may be exercised by the award holder at any time during specified months of a year within the
exercise period as set out in the grant letter. For options granted prior to the Listing, the exercise price will be
determined by the Board in its absolute discretion. For options granted after the Listing, the exercise price must
not be less than the higher of the closing price on the grant date (which must be a business day) and the average
closing price for the five business days immediately preceding the grant date.

(f) Vesting of awards: Awards vest on vesting dates specified in grant letters, subject to satisfaction of applicable
conditions. The vesting period for awards over new Shares granted after the Listing shall not be less than 12
months, except in specific circumstances including grants: (i) to new joiners to replace the share awards they
forfeited when leaving the previous employer; (ii) to award holders whose employment is terminated due to
death, ill health, serious injury, disability or retirement or upon the occurrence of any out of control event, where
the vesting of the award may accelerate based on the discretion of the Board (or the Compensation Committee,
as the case may be); (iii) with performance-based vesting conditions in lieu of time-based vesting criteria; (iv)
which could not have been made earlier due to administrative, commercial, compliance, regulatory, legal and/or
other reasons and the vesting period will be shortened to put the award holders in the same position as they
would have been in had the grant of award been made earlier; and (v) with a mixed or accelerated vesting
schedule such as where the Awards may vest evenly over a period of 12 months or pursuant to the terms and
conditions as set out in the Share Award Plan.

(g) Amounts payable on application or acceptance of award: No consideration shall be payable by the
participant on acceptance of any options, RSUs or PSUs granted under the Share Award Plan.

(h) Life of the Share Award Plan: The Share Award Plan is valid and effective for the period commencing from
adoption and expiring on the tenth (10) anniversary thereof or such earlier date as terminated by the Company or
the Board. After expiry or termination, the plan remains in effect for unvested or unexercised awards. As the
Share Award Plan was adopted on 30 January 2022, the remaining life of the Share Award Plan as at the date of
this remuneration report is approximately 5 years 9 months.

Further details of the Share Award Plan, as well as details of satisfaction by the Company of outstanding Pre-IPO
Awards granted under the Share Award Plan, are set out in the Prospectus.

During the financial year ended 31 December 2025, RSUs and PSUs were granted under the Share Award Plan,
part of which are Pre-IPO Awards. The total number of Shares that may be issued in respect of these awards
under the Share Award Plan was 11,156,111, which is approximately 0.91 per cent when divided by the weighted
average number of Shares in issue (excluding treasury shares) for the same financial year.

Employee Share Purchase Plan
The Employee Share Purchase Plan was approved and adopted by the Board on 30 January 2022 and took effect
on the Listing Date (i.e. 7 July 2025) upon satisfaction of all relevant conditions. The terms of the Employee Share
Purchase Plan have been amended by the Board on 27 February 2023 with further minor amendments made on 8
August 2024 and 16 May 2025, in each case to incorporate the requirements set out in the revised Chapter 17 of
the Listing Rules which took effect from 1 January 2023.
A summary of the key terms of the Employee Share Purchase Plan is as follows:

(a) Purpose: The purpose of the Employee Share Purchase Plan is to provide the Company with a flexible means
to retain, incentivise, reward and/or remunerate its “eligible persons” (as defined below) and drive the
performance and growth of the Group's business by providing eligible persons with the opportunity to acquire
equity interests in the Company.

(b) Participants: “Eligible persons” generally include any employee employed by: (i) a member of the Group; or
(ii) a “related entity” (as further described in the Prospectus).

(c) Maximum number of Shares available for issue: Participants who acquire the Shares under the Employee
Share Purchase Plan (Employee Purchase Shares) will be "matched" with RSUs equivalent to a specified ratio of
the Employee Purchase Shares acquired. The source of shares may be through trustee purchases on- and off-
market or through allotment and issuance of new shares. The maximum aggregate number of new Shares for
RSUs is calculated as: X = A - B - C, where A = Plan Mandate Limit, B = new Shares for RSUs already granted
under the Employee Share Purchase Plan, and C = new Shares for awards under other share-based incentive
plans. The Plan Mandate Limit may be renewed every three years subject to Shareholders' approval.

(d) Maximum entitlement of each participant under the Employee Share Purchase Plan: In any 12 month period,
the maximum number of new Shares issued and/or transferred upon (i) the vesting of RSUs granted pursuant to
the Employee Share Purchase Plan and (ii) the vesting and/or exercise of awards granted pursuant to any other
share-based incentive plans shall not exceed 1% of the Shares in issue for the time being.

(e) Vesting of RSUs: RSUs will vest in three years (or as otherwise specified) from the first day of the period which
the plan operates (which shall be of 12 months each year or a shorter period as determined by the Board in its
sole and absolute discretion) (Employee Share Purchase Plan Year). The vesting period for RSUs over new Shares
granted after the Listing shall not be less than twelve months, except in specific circumstances.

(f) Amounts payable on application or acceptance of award: The plan operates for twelve-month periods or
shorter periods as determined by the Board. Participants who enrol must participate for the full Employee Share
Purchase Plan Year. During each Employee Share Purchase Plan Year, the Board may invite participants to
acquire Employee Purchase Shares using a percentage of their monthly basic salary. The offer letter will specify
a minimum and maximum percentage of monthly basic salary that the participant may apply towards acquiring
Employee Purchase Shares under the Employee Share Purchase Plan.

(g) Life of the Employee Share Purchase Plan: The Employee Share Purchase Plan took effect upon satisfaction
of certain conditions including Board approval, approval from the listing committee of the Stock Exchange, and
commencement of trading on the main board of the Stock Exchange. The plan is valid and effective for 10 years
from satisfaction of conditions or until earlier termination. After expiry or termination, the plan remains in effect
for unvested RSUs and Employee Purchase Shares still subject to lock-up periods. As the conditions for the
Employee Share Purchase Plan were satisfied on the Listing Date (i.e. 7 July 2025), the remaining life of the
Employee Share Purchase Plan as at the date of this remuneration report is approximately 9 years 3 months.

Further details of the Employee Share Purchase Plan are set out in the Prospectus. No awards have ever been
granted under the Employee Share Purchase Plan. Accordingly, the disclosure requirements under Rule 17.07
and Rule 17.09(8) of the Listing Rules do not apply in respect of the Employee Share Purchase Plan.

Independent auditor’s report
To the shareholders of FWD Group Holdings Limited 富衛集團有限公司

(Incorporated in the Cayman Islands with limited liability)


Opinion
We have audited the consolidated financial statements of FWD Group Holdings Limited 富衛集團有限公司 (the
“Company”) and its subsidiaries (the “Group”) set out on pages 184 to 328, which comprise the consolidated
statement of financial position as at 31 December 2025, and the consolidated income statement, the
consolidated statement of comprehensive income, the consolidated statement of changes in equity and the
consolidated statement of cash flows for the year then ended, and notes to the consolidated financial
statements, including material accounting policy information.

In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements give a true and fair view of the consolidated financial
position of the Group as at 31 December 2025, and of its consolidated financial performance and its consolidated
cash flows for the year then ended in accordance with IFRS Accounting Standards and have been properly
prepared in compliance with the disclosure requirements of the Hong Kong Companies Ordinance.



Basis for opinion
We conducted our audit in accordance with International Standards on Auditing (”ISAs”). Our responsibilities
under those standards are further described in the Auditor’s responsibilities for the audit of the consolidated
financial statements section of our report. We are independent of the Group in accordance with the HKICPA’s
Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants (the “Code”), as applicable to audits of financial statements of
public interest entities. We have also fulfilled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with the Code. We
believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion.


Key audit matters
Key audit matters are those matters that, in our professional judgement, were of most significance in our audit of
the consolidated financial statements of the current period. These matters were addressed in the context of our
audit of the consolidated financial statements as a whole, and in forming our opinion thereon, and we do not
provide a separate opinion on these matters. For each matter below, our description of how our audit addressed
the matter is provided in that context.

We have fulfilled the responsibilities described in the Auditor’s responsibilities for the audit of the consolidated
financial statements section of our report, including in relation to these matters. Accordingly, our audit included
the performance of procedures designed to respond to our assessment of the risks of material misstatement of
the consolidated financial statements. The results of our audit procedures, including the procedures performed
to address the matters below, provide the basis for our audit opinion on the accompanying consolidated
financial statements.
